POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 20:11:30 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 ‘An advocate for Russia’: Kushner’s Putin comments spark outrage in Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/an-advocate-for-russia-jared-kushner-vladimir-putin-comments-spark-outrage-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 20:10:58 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9403479 Donald Trump’s peace envoy Jared Kushner this week made himself unpopular in Ukraine — and beyond.

Senior politicians in Kyiv and among Ukraine’s European allies rounded on the U.S. president’s son-in-law after he called Russian leader Vladimir Putin a “grandmaster of politics,” with a senior lawmaker in Kyiv demanding Kushner be removed from peace negotiations with Moscow.

In an interview released Wednesday on Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner’s “MD Meets” podcast, Kushner also said Putin “showed restraint” by not using nuclear weapons and stated the conflict — which the Kremlin escalated through its full-scale invasion in 2022 — had “effectively become a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia.” Like POLITICO, “MD Meets” is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

“This is extremely dangerous—not only for Ukraine but also for the security and national interests of the United States,” Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee and a lawmaker from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party, told POLITICO.

The interview offered a rare window into Kushner’s thinking as he touched on his roles in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza and his belief that “America’s most valuable export is really capitalism.”

Kushner, who described Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in the interview as an “incredible friend,” was less complimentary toward Zelenskyy, saying he had “wrongly” attacked Trump in the past.

The remarks come at a fragile moment for Kyiv’s relations with the White House. Zelenskyy is still pressing for deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles and U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi this month brought no breakthrough.

There have been persistent tensions between the U.S. and Ukrainian leaders, and Trump on Wednesday unilaterally tweaked a joint statement with NATO chief Mark Rutte to urge Ukraine, as well as Russia, to avoid expanding the war.

“I have long argued that Witkoff and Kushner need to be replaced,” Merezhko said, referring additionally to Steve Witkoff, Trump’s other peace envoy. “They view Ukraine not even as businessmen seeking deals with Russia, but through the eyes of Putin himself.”

Kushner’s framing of the conflict as a proxy war between Europe and Russia provoked the most anger in Kyiv.

It is “a complete misrepresentation of reality that, among other things, denies Ukraine’s status as an independent actor,” Halyna Yanchenko, another Servant of the People lawmaker, told POLITICO. “It seems that in this interview, Jared Kushner has in some way acted as an advocate for Russia.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the criticism of Kushner.

The interview also triggered ire among Ukraine’s staunchest backers in Europe.

Roderich Kiesewetter, a veteran German lawmaker from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, told POLITICO that Washington is “not acting as an honest broker” but is putting one-sided pressure on Ukraine. “Under Trump, the U.S. is on Russia’s side,” he said.

The White House also did not respond to a request for comment about the broader criticism of Trump.

The proxy war framing is “pure Kremlin propaganda,” said Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s security and defense committee. Kushner can “hardly be taken seriously as a neutral mediator” after the remarks, she said. The White House, she added, seemed to “rather sit on Putin’s lap than work toward a just peace.”

POLITICO contacted the foreign ministries of Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, some of Europe’s most hawkish countries on Russia, for comment on Kushner’s remarks but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

For Yanchenko, the Ukrainian Servant of the People MP, the bigger risk is that Washington believes what it hears in Moscow. 

“In my opinion, talk of warmer relations is a myth that Putin is trying to make the American negotiating team believe,” she said.

]]> en Meta’s UK rollout for Muse AI agent exposes it to more liability https://www.politico.eu/article/metas-uk-rollout-for-muse-ai-agent-exposes-it-to-more-liability/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 11:25:07 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9396576 LONDON — Meta will be on the hook for more of Muse’s mistakes in the U.K. than in the U.S., according to a comparison of the AI agent’s fine print in both countries by POLITICO.

Following conversations with regulators, Muse’s terms of service give British consumers more scope to seek redress if the personal AI agent makes mistakes compared with users in the U.S.

The findings indicate the tech giant was willing to commit to meeting higher liability standards to gain access to the U.K. market, and show that tech companies and users will face different liability and consumer law rules as personal AI agents roll out globally.

Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators.

The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law.

Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.”

The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval.

The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.”

They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.”

In the U.K. there is no financial cap and a narrower list of exceptions to Meta’s liability applies only where the company has “acted with reasonable skill and care / professional diligence.”

Under U.K. consumer law, this standard is automatically implied into contracts for services between a business and a consumer. How U.K. consumers would fare in practice when seeking redress for any problems caused by personal AI agents is yet to be tested in court.

Since its debut in the U.S., Meta staffers have reportedly raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” by the agent, from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases. (A Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”)

The CMA said it expects Muse to be the first of many personal AI agents to come to the U.K. and has invited users to report any issues they experience with personal AI agents.

Other British regulators are also watching closely. The Financial Conduct Authority said in a statement that as AI agents become capable of making transactions, payments and investment decisions, companies developing and deploying them “must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply.”

It also highlighted that a broad Consumer Duty could also apply to regulated firms’ use of AI agents, and that all companies must decide carefully whether they should accept payments initiated by an agent.

As well as contract law, consumer law, negligence and sector-specific regulation, users of AI agents may soon also be able to seek redress through product liability laws.

The Law Commission is reviewing the U.K.’s product liability laws and has proposed extending the definition to software, including AI. Doing so could make firms developing or deploying AI agents strictly liable for certain types of harm they cause.

The 12-nation trade alliance, also known as the CPTPP, agreed to establish three working groups to handle the negotiations, which could lead to its biggest expansion to date.

Countries joining the alliance must commit to sweeping tariff liberalization as well as opening up digital trade.

Accession talks with Uruguay, which have been running since early this year, are well advanced and could “potentially” be concluded early next year, a diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the plans told POLITICO.

Trade ministers are meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, for the 11th CPTPP Commission meeting, hosted annually by a rotating chair.

The U.K. became the first country without a Pacific coastline to join the bloc in 2024. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico and Singapore were among its founding members in 2018. Decisions are taken by consensus.

The U.K. is expected to sign a trade deal soon with the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE. But London has yet to strike trade deals with the fast-growing Indonesian and Philippine economies.

Negotiations with the three nations “are all complicated and will require serious effort to get across the line,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation think tank. “This includes capacity building for some applicants to make certain that everyone is clear on what the CPTPP requires, as well as careful work to ensure that member concerns are addressed.”

The bloc is emerging as a “Plan B” as efforts to reform the World Trade Organization falter. China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Ukraine, Cambodia and Argentina have also applied to join.

]]> en The man who coined ‘Brexit’ likes the sound of ‘Breturn’ and ‘Brejoin’ https://www.politico.eu/article/the-man-who-coined-brexit-likes-the-sound-of-breturn-and-brejoin-peter-wilding/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 10:32:43 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9395349 LONDON — The political strategist credited with first using the term Brexit says it’s too early to predict slogans for a future referendum — but rates Breturn and Brejoin as potential portmanteaux.

Peter Wilding, a consultant based in Brussels, told POLITICO that the political landscape has shifted since 2016 when Brits voted to leave the EU and that pro-EU campaign rhetoric will have to change to keep up.

His comments come as U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reopens the conversation on Britain’s relationship with Europe, and campaigners on both sides of the debate regroup in preparation for a potential second fight over bloc membership.

Since arriving in Downing Street, Burnham has argued that Brexit “has not worked” as he tees up tighter ties with the EU. He has said that he hopes to rejoin within his lifetime — but insisted Monday that it would be “unthinkable” to do so without a referendum.

“If you’re looking for something catchy, there’s a couple of options: Let’s Breturn or Brejoin,” Wilding said when asked what the moniker for a future campaign should be. “But really, Burnham doesn’t want to go back to the past, he wants to go to the future, and the faces and arguments of 2016 will be dumped.”

“There will be a tonal change where Burnham caters his argument towards the younger vote and the business vote — seizing these cohorts will be vital to electoral success,” the strategist added.

Wilding coined Brexit in 2012 when he penned an article on Britain’s place in Europe.

“Unless a clear view is pushed that Britain must lead in Europe at the very least to achieve the completion of the single market, then the portmanteau for Greek euro exit might be followed by another sad word, Brexit,” he wrote for news outlet Euractiv , now known as Rapporteur. His writing is cited as the earliest evidence of the word Brexit in the Oxford English Dictionary.

The term was subsequently adopted as the accepted shorthand for the U.K. leaving Europe and was plastered on buses and billboards during the 2016 referendum campaign on Britain’s membership.

Having a snappy way of encapsulating the Vote Leave argument — and catchy slogans to go alongside — was crucial in building the campaign in the public imagination, Wilding said.

“The Take Back Control control slogan was an absolute winner.”

As Burnham gears up to set out different options for the U.K.-EU relationship, Wilding argued that the British prime minister has already got the upper hand on the opposition by co-opting the winning slogans of the past.

“Burnham has found the two best weapons from the 2016 campaign: take back control and immigration, and he has occupied that territory,” he said, pointing to the Labour leader’s party conference speech in September .

The PM told supporters in Liverpool: “The British Right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place.”

Wilding said that Burnham’s gradual approach to deepening Britain’s ties with Brussels is “flushing out” the opposition — who he claimed look “splutteringly indignant” when they trot out 2016-era arguments that have been disproved.

“Burnham is tackling the immigration argument head on,” Wilding said. “He can say you won that referendum on immigration and the Boriswave threw your credibility away and because of that you don’t have an argument to make” — a term coined by the online right to describe the increase in migration under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s Conservative government following the pandemic.

Nigel Farage, a key architect of the campaign to pull the U.K. out of the EU, announced Wednesday that he is launching a new effort Keep Britain Out.

“There will be a lot of online battling,” Wilding said. “But the only leader is Burnham himself, and what he says and does will affect the development of the Get In and Stay Out campaigns.”

On the question of whether the public is ready for another full-blown campaign, the Brexit-coiner said: “I don’t think they are. I think we are in the team talk period before the match begins and anything can happen in the next year.”

]]> en Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ? https://www.politico.eu/article/ue-tech-americaine-dependance-souverainete-ia-cloud/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:41:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9396768 BRUXELLES — Même si l’UE est unie dans sa volonté de réduire sa dépendance aux technologies américaines, chaque Etat membre devra se débrancher de son côté — et certains auront bien plus d’efforts à fournir que d’autres.

Une étude menée par des chercheurs finlandais a mis en évidence de grandes disparités dans le degré de dépendance des Etats européens envers Amazon, Microsoft et Google pour les services publics numériques destinés aux citoyens.

“Cette variation n’est pas aléatoire, elle est systématique”, explique Vili Lehdonvirta, professeur de politique technologique à l’université finlandaise Aalto et coauteur du rapport.

Les chercheurs ont analysé les sites web gouvernementaux de 158 pays — notamment les portails permettant aux citoyens de trouver des informations, de déposer des demandes et d’effectuer des démarches administratives — afin d’évaluer dans quelle mesure ceux-ci dépendent des trois géants de la tech américaine.

Au sein de l’UE, Malte, la Finlande et l’Irlande affichent les parts les plus élevées de services publics nationaux hébergés par des hyperscalers américains : respectivement 78,5%, 56,1% et 45,8%.

En revanche, le taux estimé pour la France est de 9,3%, comparé à 2,9% pour l’Allemagne.

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que l’UE négocie actuellement un projet de législation qui obligerait les administrations publiques à revoir leurs achats de solutions digitales américaines, dans un contexte marqué par les menaces répétées de Washington contre les politiques numériques de Bruxelles, de tentatives locales de se passer des services américains et les récentes pannes ayant affecté des outils informatiques très répandus.

Selon l’étude, Bahreïn présente le plus fort degré de dépendance au monde, les services américains hébergeant 81% des sites étudiés, tandis que la Russie et la Chine ne comptent aucun site public lié aux trois géants de la tech.

Les chercheurs ont constaté que les disparités dans le recours aux Big Tech tendent à être liées à la taille d’un pays et au coût du travail.

“L’explication est d’ordre économique : dans un grand pays, le marché domestique est mieux à même de soutenir des alternatives ou des technologies nationales, qui impliquent des investissements importants et des économies d’échelle élevées”, a détaillé Vili Lehdonvirta.

Pourquoi la taille compte

En Europe, la carte de la dépendance aux technologies américaines suit des tendances similaires, reflétant la taille du marché et le niveau de revenu. Cependant, elle est également plus contrastée en raison d’un ensemble hétéroclite de choix nationaux qui complique les efforts de l’UE visant à réduire ces dépendances stratégiques.

“Dans l’ensemble, on a cette configuration où les petits Etats membres ont recours au cloud américain et pas les grands Etats membres”, a décrit Vili Lehdonvirta. “Le cloud est un exemple de technologie qui nécessite un investissement initial important, et ensuite, plus on opère à grande échelle, plus elle est efficace.”

La méthodologie de l’étude présente certaines limites pour évaluer le degré de dépendance globale, car elle se concentre uniquement sur l’hébergement des services nationaux destinés au grand public, et non sur les systèmes locaux ni sur l’utilisation plus large de la technologie au sein de l’administration. Par exemple, Vili Lehdonvirta indique que les entités municipales — tels que les conseils d’école ou les systèmes de billetterie des piscines — sont plus susceptibles de recourir à des technologies américaines, la souveraineté numérique ne relevant pas de leurs compétences.

La taille et les revenus ne font pas tout non plus : les choix politiques déterminent également si les pays développent ou non des fournisseurs nationaux.

Au Royaume-Uni — la cinquième puissance mondiale —, 50,9% des sites gouvernementaux dépendent de technologies américaines, selon l’étude. Vili Lehdonvirta rappelle que l’exécutif britannique “a décidé, il y a environ quinze ans, de mettre le paquet sur le cloud dans le cadre d’une directive du gouvernement s’appliquant à tous les ministères et agences gouvernementales”. En l’absence d’alternatives nationales, “très rapidement, tout a migré vers le cloud américain. Aujourd’hui, il serait difficile de revenir en arrière, même s’ils le souhaitaient”, souligne-t-il.

De nouvelles règles à venir

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que les responsables politiques à Bruxelles débattent pour savoir où fixer les limites : les nouvelles règles proposées — dans le Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) — devraient-elles obliger les administrations publiques à réaliser des tests de souveraineté et à se tourner vers des alternatives européennes pour les secteurs les plus sensibles, ce qui pourrait évincer les géants américains de la tech ?

Rien que dans le secteur privé, les entreprises européennes dépensent environ 330 milliards d’euros par an en services cloud et logiciels américains, ce qui confère à la tech américaine une part de marché estimée à 83% selon une étude de 2025.

Mais les Etats membres n’ont pas tous intérêt à des règles strictes en la matière. Cela dépend en partie s’ils ont ou non des fournisseurs nationaux prêts à rivaliser.

Josh Kallmer, directeur des affaires internationales chez Zoom, dont le siège est aux Etats-Unis, estime pour sa part que l’échelon européen est le bon niveau pour agir, car il permettrait d’éviter des règles différentes dans chaque pays. “Cette divergence supplémentaire affecte une entreprise comme la nôtre”, a-t-il déclaré lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO. “Chaque restriction supplémentaire mise en place a un impact beaucoup plus important sur la liberté de choix dans les pays de taille moyenne et les petits pays.”

Les négociateurs du CADA en sont pleinement conscients. “Nous devons essayer de mettre en place un cadre clair afin que les 27 pays aient la même interprétation de la loi, car, en fin de compte, le but est de faciliter la tâche des PME en Europe”, dit Diego Solier, eurodéputé membre des Conservateurs et réformistes européens, qui est l’un des principaux négociateurs sur ce dossier.

Pour le coauteur de l’étude, Vili Lehdonvirta, ce texte risque de rater sa cible s’il ne répartit pas plus équitablement les coûts et avantages au sein de l’UE.

“Le coût de la mise en conformité de cette politique pèse principalement sur les petits Etats membres, tandis que ses avantages, à savoir l’augmentation de l’activité économique, profitent surtout aux grands Etats membres”, développe-t-il. “Si nous ne disposons d’aucun mécanisme de partage des charges, le résultat final sera similaire à ce que nous observons actuellement, c’est-à-dire une sorte de tentative timide qui n’oblige pas vraiment qui que ce soit à agir.”

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Among Europe’s “patriotic” parties, “it is not the AfD that is isolated, but increasingly the National Rally, if it carries on like this,” she added.

Weidel dismissed the suggestion that a Russian victory would trigger another wave of refugees heading west. “There will be no refugee movement. Quite the opposite,” she said, arguing that Ukrainians in Germany would return home once peace was established “because they are needed there.”

]]> en Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans https://www.politico.eu/article/bank-of-england-boss-warns-ai-must-benefit-humans/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 27 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9397860 LONDON — Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned governments need to reassure the public about the benefits of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models, amid rising fears the technology is advancing at a pace beyond human control.

As the U.K. prepares to take over the G20 presidency, Bailey backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plan to put AI at the heart of the country’s plans.

But the U.K. central banker said lawmakers, not regulators, would have to set the guardrails for the technology.

“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as “super intelligence.”

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

But the governor argued it was reasonable for the public to ask what the benefit is from the rapid growth of a technology which could be used to blow holes in the financial system, but also order the Christmas shopping.

“The public needs to trust this technology,” he said. “There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.”

He added: “It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.”

The U.K. central banker is acutely aware of the threats the new technology could bring to the financial system. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee report on Thursday spelled out risks including increasingly interconnected and opaque financing that could spread the pain should a potential stock market AI bubble burst.

But Bailey said he would put himself in a camp of people who want AI to succeed to improve productivity and well-being.

“But it has to be under human control,” he said. “We want AI to be used by humans, as it were.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:45:31 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 From housing, to migration, Gaza, renewables and the far-right: the bigger picture behind Spain’s Sunday election https://euobserver.com/252246/from-housing-to-migration-gaza-renewables-and-the-far-right-the-bigger-picture-behind-spains-sunday-election/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:09:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=252246 A People's Party-Vox coalition of the centre-right and far-right will reshape Madrid’s stance on migration, Israel, and climate policy, while shifting Spain closer to Europe’s increasingly rightwing political mainstream.]]> Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday (29 November) in a high-stakes snap election that could end prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s eight years in power.

Sánchez became prime minister in June 2018 through a no-confidence motion, and after a repeat election in November 2019 he formed Spain’s first coalition government since the return to democracy, with the leftwing Podemos, one of the new parties that emerged after the financial crisis.

Polls from Monday (23 November) suggest the centre-right People’s Party (PP), on 31.4 percent, and far-right Vox, on 17.9 percent, could win a majority and form a coalition government, ahead of the Sánchez’s Socialist Party (PSOE) (29.1 percent) and the lefwing Frente Amplio [Broad Front] plus coalitions with Podemos and others (6.8 percent).

Support for Sánchez’s PSOE in the polls is now roughly similar to back in 2019, but the major difference is Vox has grown, driven largely by young voters frustrated over housing and living costs

Meanwhile, Sánchez faces criticism from within his own party.

One former Socialist prime minister, Felipe González, who led Spain from 1982 to 1996, has said he will not vote for Sánchez, accusing him of compromising with Catalan and Basque separatists.

Nearly 39 million people are eligible to vote on Sunday, according to Spain’s statistics institute, and around 2.8 million of them live abroad — with many seen in social media posts queuing for hours to cast their votes in consulates across the globe. 

Postal voting — which can be used by both those living abroad and at home — has been especially politicised this time, with leaders of the PP and Vox, including Madrid’s regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, doubting its legitimacy and urging people to vote in person.

During a debate on Thursday evening, when Sánchez pressed PP leader and frontrunner Alberto Núñez Feijóo on whether he would accept the result, Feijóo dodged the question, instead pledging to resign if he failed to become prime minister and challenging Sánchez to do the same.

Domestically, the campaign has been dominated by the housing crisis, but the cost of living, corruption cases, this summer’s migration crisis in Ceuta and the train crash that killed 69 people near Toledo in October have also shaped the debate.

And despite Sánchez’s high international profile, as one of the continent’s most powerful centre-left leaders, foreign policy has been mostly secondary in this campaign.

But it is clear that a change in government could reshape certain aspects of Spain’s stand in Brussels and beyond.

Will Frederiksen miss Sánchez?

Under Sánchez, Spain pursued a mass regularisation of undocumented migrants, a policy several EU leaders pointedly criticised over the past few months as a pull factor for irregular migration.

Spain was also the only member state to vote against the EU’s new return rules in December 2025, as Sánchez has been one of Europe’s most vocal opponents of “return hubs”, deportation centres outside the EU, putting him at odds with leaders such as Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni.

Read more

Denmark lashes out again at Sánchez over Spain’s migration regularisation, but EU summit avoids linking migration to crime

But a PP-Vox government would bring Spain closer to the European mainstream on these issues.

After this summer’s Ceuta migration crisis, Brussels avoided assigning Morocco specific blame, insisting instead that Rabat remains a key partner of the EU. 

Some 80,000 people unexpectedly crossed into the Spanish enclave over two days in late July, and while the European Commission offered Spain emergency funding and called the images “unacceptable”, it rejected calls to freeze EU support for Morocco and confirmed that money for Moroccan border work would keep flowing. 

That position may be hard to square with a future PP-Vox government, since the hard-right Vox has repeatedly pointed the finger at Rabat.

Feijóo has said he wants good relations with Morocco but he has also used as a camping slogan the idea that “Ceuta is Not for Sale”. The party’s manifesto relies on readmissions by Morocco, which actually requires Rabat’s cooperation. 

The socialist voice amplifying Gaza’s suffering 

On the Middle East, Sánchez’s departure would silence one of the strongest critics of the EU’s relations with Israel, as the socialist leader has been praised for condemning the humanitarian situation in Gaza and calling on Israel to respect international law.

As for US president Donald Trump, Sánchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have stood up to him, criticising some of his policies, against what diplomats described as the EU’s instinctive response of doing everything possible to keep Trump happy. 

Sánchez refused to support the proposed ramp-up in Nato defence spending last year. But the relationship with Washington worsened in March, when Sánchez’s coalition denied US requests to allow use of the jointly operated Rota and Morón military bases in Spain for attacks on Iran.

Read more

Sanchez’s snap election, and what his defeat would mean for Spain’s Nato spending

However, when it comes to Russia’s war in Ukraine, political scientists argue that despite the possibility of having Vox in government, it is unlikely to change Madrid’s stance.

Camino Mortera-Martínez, a Spanish analyst and fellow of the think tank Centre for European Reform (CER), has argued that Vox “will be happier with ‘extracting’ concessions on things like Morocco and Israel than Ukraine”.

She also said that coalition allies of Sánchez such as Podemos have “harder views on Russia than Vox”.

Podemos has strongly opposed arms shipments since 2022, favouring instead a negotiated settlement with Russia. During the campaign, Podemos candidate and MEP Irene Montero claimed that Western weapons sent to Ukraine were being used by the Azov brigade to train Spanish neo-Nazi group Núcleo Nacional, but Ukraine’s embassy in Madrid denied it.

Green rollback

With a Vox-PP government in power, Spain’s climate policies are also likely to undergo a dramatic change. The PP and Vox want to stop the nuclear phase-out timetable, while Vox is seeking to roll back any Green Deal-related policies. 

During Thursday’s televised debate, far-right leader Santiago Abascal talked against “climate fanaticism” while arguing Spain should resume exploring its fossil-fuel resources.

“Jobs are being lost, and this is down to the Green Deal and Mercosur policies – approved in this case by the Socialist Party and the People’s Party in Brussels – which promise us a green future, but which is a bleak future for millions of people who are struggling terribly,” Abascal said.

Actually, analysts such as Ember say that Spain’s renewable expansion has reduced exposure to gas price shocks and lowered electricity costs (in the first half of 2025, Spanish wholesale prices were 32 percent lower than the EU average). 

In recent years, Spain has seen its wind and solar capacity double, adding over 40 GW, more than any EU country except Germany — which has a power market is roughly twice the size of Spain’s. 

But in line with recent demands from the European People’s Party, Feijóo has pledged that, if he wins the elections, Spain will join the Austria-led regulatory moratorium, backed by 15 other member states. 

Vox likely to get farming, family, or culture  

Vox, which was founded in 2013 by dissatisfied ex-hardliners from the PP, would be the first far-right party to enter a Spanish government since the country’s return to democracy in 1978. 

Spanish media report that Vox could take the agriculture ministry in a possible coalition government, along with family or culture, and perhaps a vice-presidency linked to deregulation.

Agriculture has become one of Vox’s main political battlegrounds, with the party presenting itself as the defender of Spanish farmers, and it already runs the agriculture departments in PP-led regional governments such as Extremadura, Aragón and Castilla y León.

But for several years now, far-right parties have been gaining ground in many European countries.  

Italy is led by the hard-right, Belgium is led by a conservative-nationalist, while far-right parties are junior coalition partners in countries like Finland, Croatia and Slovakia. 

In Sweden, the far-right Sweden Democrats were supporting Stockholm’s minority government from 2022 until this autumn’s election.

Meanwhile, in countries like Germany and Portugal, there is a (fraying) ‘cordon sanitaire’, or firewall, that keeps the AfD and Chega outside of government. 

“The integration of parts of the far-right into the EU’s political system is already well advanced and continues to grow,” according to a report by the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP, German Institute for International and Security Afffairs) reflecting on the “creeping” integration of far-right parties in Europe.  

Amnesty International has warned that the PP and Vox manifestos contain clear setbacks for human rights, mostly on migration, housing and the right to protest, including plans for faster deportations, a “Spaniards first” rule for public housing and benefits, and the repeal of Spain’s rent-control law.

]]> Amazon workers mobilise on Black Friday to demand better pay and conditions https://euobserver.com/252295/amazon-workers-mobilise-on-black-friday-to-demand-better-pay-and-conditions/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:40:57 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=252295 Amazon workers across Europe join global protests, demanding collective agreements, decent pay, and healthy working conditions in a yearly push against the giant corporation.]]> Amazon workers across Europe joined global protests on Friday (27 November), demanding collective agreements, decent pay, and healthy working conditions in a yearly push against the giant corporation.

Some 11 German working sites, one in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland, and the UK joined their peers around the world demanding the right to organise in labour unions, protection from abusive surveillance, and less performance pressure.

Their actions come on Black Friday, the most profitable day in the calendar for the firm, as they demand that workers also get a fair share.

“Amazon is building a future in which fewer workers produce ever greater profits under ever tighter surveillance,” Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla, coordinator of Progressive International, organising the protest movement said in a statement. The annual protests seek to show the firm they “are not invincible.”

Amazon employs more than 230,000 people and contracts another 40,000 in Europe, most working on packing and delivering customer orders. The firm already earned $742.8bn in 2026, making it the world’s second largest company after JPMorgan Chase, ranked by sales, profits, assets, and market value.

“We’re fighting against this kind of company that tramples on workers’ rights,” said Leïla Chaibi, a French left-wing MEP, in a social media statement backing the campaign.

Read more

Digital panopticon: ‘When you work faster, you have to work even faster’ Amazon workers tell MEPs on AI work surveillance

“We want to make Amazon start paying for the costs linked with its revenues,” Magda Malinowska, from the Polish labour union Inicjatywa Pracownicza, told EUobserver. These include covering healthcare costs for its workers.

“Then it’s the society that supports people who are unable to work because they’ve damaged their joints or backs” working at Amazon, she said.

Since the Polish law on strikes is one of the most restrictive in Europe, Malinowska said, unions have been campaigning to change it to be able to pressure Amazon. “We have had other demands for a million years but they will hardly be listened to if we cannot strike,” she said.

In Frankenthal, Germany, some 150 workers stopped for 24 hours to demand less performance pressure and the right to join a collective agreement for retail workers, David Koch, secretary of the local labour union Ver.di told EUobserver.

Read more

Unions rally against new ‘EU Inc’ race-to-bottom on labour laws and pay

Even though the strike is legal, managers “give workers a feeling” that there will be consequences if they join the strike, even though they cannot threaten them directly, Koch said. 

In response to the union actions, Amazon representatives said in late 2025 that the firm “provides great pay, great benefits, and great opportunities—all from day one.”

In 2025, it lost its lobbying pass to the European parliament after it did not show up to an employment committee hearing in January about working conditions in its warehouses. In October, a committee delegation visited its site to investigate.

“Amazon makes a show of being transparent,” by opening their warehouses, but gives ”no real answers for our questions,” said Estelle Ceulemans, a Belgian socialist MEP, reporting back from the visit on 9 November.

]]> Airlines bankroll travel influencers — and normalise a high‑carbon lifestyle for Europeans https://euobserver.com/252204/airlines-bankroll-travel-influencers-and-normalise-a-highcarbon-lifestyle-for-europeans/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:03:34 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=252204 Influencers can sell a glamorised lifestyle without it looking like an ad, and consumers are fooled. Though airlines get the win, the effects of over-tourism, climate deterioration, and basic legal transparency are increasingly difficult to ignore. ]]> Travel influencers are selling a glamourised lifestyle to consumers without sufficient transparency or control – and with a dire price tag for the climate.

A report by Berlin-based T3 Transportation think tank on Thursday (26 November) shows that constant posting of photogenic locations shapes consumers’ destination preferences, inciting long-distance flying, fuelling air travel demand, accelerating over-tourism, and contributing to climate change. 

Airlines’ PR strategies have increasingly relied on the so-called ‘disguised advertiser‘. That means aspirational trip content posted by online creators creeps into online feeds more smoothly than traditional advertising – and seem to pull in a significant audience.

In concrete numbers, content creators take an average of 16 flights per year, visiting four times as many destinations and generating a climate impact 16.7 times higher than the average European’s four leisure round trips a year – “creating and normalising a desire for frequent, long-haul flying,” said Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, aviation campaigner at advocacy group European Federation for Transport and Environment.

Read more

Social media influencers now roam EU corridors of power: free trips, selfies with leaders but a grey zone for ethics

“However, influencer posts often fail to disclose that they are paid promotions by airlines,” Rodrigues Akhtar told EUobserver.

The report estimated that about one-third of digital advertising budget in airlines is spent on social media in 2025, with low-cost flyer Easyjet leading the charts at €10m.

“Consumers often do not realise that they are being targeted by marketing and rarely given a balanced picture of the environmental cost,” said the European consumer organisation’s (BEUC) head of consumer rights, Patrycja Gautier.

]]> Swedish Gripen jets with Meteor missiles will arrive in Ukraine in January, posing the first serious threat to Russian aviation (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,737) https://euobserver.com/252231/swedish-gripen-jets-with-meteor-missiles-will-arrive-in-ukraine-in-january-posing-the-first-serious-threat-to-russian-aviation-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1737/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:18:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=252231 A war that has already emptied towns like Avdiivka and sent villagers herding cows to safety may be on the verge of its most dramatic shift yet.]]>
  • Why the new weapon is a threat, especially to the Su-34.
  • What the Su-34 means for the Russian air force.
  • Komar is already under Ukrainian control; the attack on Velyka Novosilka continues.
  • Russia has spent €206bn on weapons and ammunition alone since the start of the invasion.
  • Ukraine could lose almost €9bn a year as a result of the blockade of Black Sea ports.
  • How Russia is destroying Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
  • Maps of the day — the distribution of attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure from August to October; Komar and the Velyka Novosilka direction.
  • Videos of the day — Avdiivka three years after its “liberation” by the Russians; a Ukrainian soldier saw his children after four months; rural residents rescue their livestock.

    • Why the new weapon is a threat, especially to the Su-34. “A manoeuvrable fighter. We have flown against such aircraft over the Baltic Sea. Under current conditions, most of them will be destroyed on the ground,” Russian pilot Ilya Tumanov (Fighterbomber) wrote tersely and confidently in May, when it was confirmed that Ukraine would receive 16 Gripen C/D fighter jets from Sweden.

    The Czech and Hungarian air forces operate the same version. Sweden is gradually switching to the E/F version, which Ukrainians are also expected to receive by the end of the decade.

    Tumanov’s assessment was wrong, first because Russia has not destroyed a single F-16 or Mirage 2000 on the ground to date — or at least nothing of the sort is known. If Russia had proof, it would immediately have publicised it. There is therefore no reason to assume that the situation will be dramatically different with the Gripens.

    The second problem with his argument is that while Gripens are indeed agile aircraft, their greatest significance for the course of the air war will probably lie in the fact that Meteor air-to-air missiles will arrive on the battlefield with them.

    This is at a time when warnings of the next blitzkrieg bombard us daily while our leaders seem to ‘whistle past the graveyard’ (an English saying for being complacent in the face of death.)

    We have some wonderful entertainment, exceptional writers and actors, and more ways to watch their work than any previous generation. There is some fine drama about social injustice and the pressures of daily life.

    But across our broadcasters and the global platforms, there is remarkably little sustained exploration of the crises that will shape our children’s future.

    Audiences are not indifferent.

    A 2026 Eurobarometer survey found that 72 percent of EU citizens are highly worried about active conflicts and wars near Europe’s borders, and more than two-thirds believe their own country is under threat.

    Read more

    Nuclear weapons – the elephant in the room in Ukraine peace talks

    These are the circumstances in which our viewers live. Journalism establishes the facts, investigates wrongdoing, and holds power to account, sometimes at the cost of journalists’ lives.

    Drama completes that work. It can take us inside a family, a workplace, or a negotiating room, and expose the distance between what people say they believe and what they do when those beliefs become costly.

    And it can imagine where they might lead, bringing consequences into view before they become tomorrow’s news.

    Proud history of TV dramas

    British television once did this superbly. Cathy Come Home brought homelessness into the living room through one young family’s disintegration. Boys from the Blackstuff explored unemployment through the dignity, humour, and despair of men whose working lives had collapsed.

    In 1984, Threads imagined nuclear war through its consequences for Sheffield, asking what the language of deterrence would mean for ordinary streets, hospitals, and families. Its terror came from recognising the world being destroyed. 

    That same year, Edgar Reitz’s landmark German series Heimat proved just how powerfully this kind of storytelling can resonate across borders. Following the quiet village of Schabbach as it was gradually seduced into fascism and war through the promise of economic progress, the series became a huge critical and popular success – showing millions of viewers how ordinary neighbours slowly normalise and comply with an approaching catastrophe.

    That tradition was never easy: the BBC withheld The War Game, its own film about a nuclear attack, from television for 20 years. Nor has ambition disappeared. ITV’s Mr Bates vs the Post Office drew an average audience of 14 million, turning years of journalism into a national reckoning.

    Netflix’s Adolescence won eight Emmys; Chernobyl, HBO and Sky’s drama of institutional lies and nuclear disaster, won 10. The producers behind Adolescence have now acquired the rights to a new adaptation of Threads.

    That is welcome, but one project cannot answer the wider question.

    Our public service broadcasters air hundreds of hours of new British drama every year. Surely there is room within it for a sustained commitment to the threats that hang over us all.

    The obstacles are real. Broadcasters face falling revenues and fierce competition from global platforms. A story that matters profoundly to domestic viewers can struggle to raise money across many markets. Even Mr Bates, sold to 12 overseas broadcasters, had reportedly lost ITV around £1m [€1.2m] by April 2024.

    Independent producers often have to surrender most of their rights to a major platform to get a series made, losing the returns that would fund the next ambitious project.

    There is no silver bullet solution, but there are pockets of progress throughout Europe.

    Five Nordic public broadcasters pooled their drama co-production through Nordic12, explicitly to sustain their cultures amid global competition. Joined by Germany’s ZDF, the Netherlands’ NPO and Belgium’s VRT, they now form New8, renewed in January for another three years.

    The UK should build similar partnerships with European and Canadian broadcasters, sharing development, financing, and access to programmes.

    Read more

    Europe is losing the algorithmic war for streaming – and that’s a policy failure

    Governments, which have named the creative industries a priority for growth, should help independent companies keep a stake in their own work.

    And the debate over the BBC’s next charter is an immediate chance to make distinctive drama about our shared uncertainties an explicit part of its purpose.

    But better financing only makes such drama possible; commissioners must still choose to back it.

    The devastation in Gaza, the conflict involving Iran and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, give our anxieties a terrible human reality.

    The possibility of nuclear war is openly discussed. Behind every report are families living with bereavement, displacement and fear. Studios and broadcasters can treat these threats as too bleak, too political, or too hard to sell.

    Or they can recognise that loyalty, power, fear, and responsibility to our children are the oldest dramatic subjects, and that they have never mattered more.

    Drama with purpose can entertain us, confront what we share and help us understand what this would mean for our families and friendships, and help us recognise what is at stake while there is still time to act.

    But to tell these stories, we must preserve an independent European industry with the ambition and courage to make them, and the determination to reflect our values.

    As Telex reports, critics argue that the new tax could drive capital out of Hungary, divert funds from investment, impose a heavy administrative burden and affect many owners of smaller businesses.  

    It remains unclear whether president András Baka will sign the bill into law.

    KATA scheme revamped

    Another major tax change is parliament’s approval of the return of KATA, a simplified tax scheme for small businesses.

    In the summer of 2022, the Fidesz government changed the rules so that most self-employed people could no longer use it. The move provoked widespread anger just months after Orbán and his party won their biggest election victory.

    The Tisza government has now made it possible for self-employed people who invoice companies to use KATA. People who run a business alongside their main job will also be eligible again.

The European Court of Auditors interrogated the disbursement of funds in Germany, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Portugal and Poland.]]> Controls implemented by the EU failed to ensure money from so-called ‘green bonds’ was invested in environmentally-beneficial projects, with some of the funds spent on oil- and gas-fuelled assets.

    That’s according to a report published on Wednesday (25 November) by the European Court of Auditors, showing that the bloc’s environmental expenditure was sometimes not green, and that at other times the money could not be traced.

    Green bonds were issued by the EU Commission to help finance NextGenerationEU (NGEU), a recovery and resilience fund for post-Covid economic growth. 

    Out of 60 projects reviewed by auditors, eight materially overstated green spending, with auditors estimating that across seven member states, an estimated €5.5bn (9.8 percent) of €56.8bn may have been overstated.

    Issuing the bonds made the EU a major issuer of green debt, and bloc rules require member states to use at least 37 percent of their recovery money on sustainability. “We have identified ways to strengthen the existing framework [… ] This could also be important if the EU decides to issue green bonds again,” said lead auditor Jorg Kristijan Petrovič.

    In 2023, the European Green Bond Standard (EuGBS) was adopted by the EU as part of new green regulations. But since NGEU bonds began to be issued in 2021, this money was never the subject of new sustainable financing rules.

    The fact that bond spending did not meet the commission’s own standards “may create a perception of inconsistency,” according to the audit.

    “[The commission’s] own NGEU green bonds are not fully aligned with the EuGBS’s more stringent requirements,” the audit found. It also said there is no target for NGEU green bonds to align fully with the EU taxonomy in the future.

    ]]>         Lula’s online ‘army’ shows how copying Brazil’s WhatsApp model could backfire on Spain and France’s left https://euobserver.com/251777/lulas-online-army-shows-how-copying-brazils-whatsapp-model-could-backfire-on-spains-and-frances-left/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:00:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251777 With Spain voting on Sunday and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian 'digital army' experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right's dominance of online political communication. But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula's victory, his online army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.]]> Europe’s Left believes it may have found a formula for defeating the far-right.

    Following Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election last month, progressive movements in France and Spain began replicating the digital mobilisation strategy developed by congressman André Janones, whose WhatsApp channel, Exército do Lula (Lula’s Army), attracted nearly 11 million followers.

    With Spain voting on Sunday (29 November) and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right’s dominance of online political communication. 

    But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula’s victory, his digital army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.

    The channel that once mobilised millions against Bolsonaro is now being used to attack leftwing politicians and activists who oppose the government’s proposed fiscal adjustment – that was swiftly approved with the full support of the far-right.

    Read more

    Trump cheers Bolsonaro Jr’s advance on Lula in Brazil, but EU fears for Mercosur alliance

    Among its targets are members of the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), that supported the re-election of Lula da Silva, critics concerned about the potential consequences of fiscal restraint for public services and the poor, and even politicians of the president’s own Workers’ Party (PT).

    Janones has accused sections of the left of sabotaging Lula’s government, while more than 1.4 million followers have reportedly abandoned his channel since the election.

    The irony is difficult to ignore as a digital instrument celebrated for defending democracy against authoritarianism and the dangers of a new far-right government is now being deployed to discourage legitimate democratic disagreement.

    Lessons for Europe

    And this is precisely what European progressives should be examining before rushing to import Janones’ methods.

    There is no denying the effectiveness of his electoral strategy since through carefully coordinated messaging, viral content and instructions to millions of followers, Janones helped challenge Flavio Bolsonaro’s formidable digital machinery.

    Yet the electoral success of this operation should not obscure its fundamental limitations: mobilising millions of people to distribute political messages is not the same as empowering them to participate in political decisions.

    What happens when the candidate wins? Are those supporters expected to continue following orders, defending every government decision, regardless of their political convictions?

    That appears to be the contradiction confronting Lula’s Army.

    Its followers were instrumentalised as political combatants, receiving instructions about what to share, amplify and attack but they were never part of a democratic organisation capable of collectively deciding its political direction.

    When supporters began expressing dissatisfaction with Lula’s fiscal proposals, many responded to messages with scissors emojis, symbolising their opposition to potential spending cuts. Rather than engaging with their objections, Janones turned against critics within the left.

    It is an especially troubling development considering the historical relationship between Lula’s Workers’ Party and competing leftwing movements.

    In 2003, the PT expelled parliamentarians who opposed Lula’s pension reform, helping precipitate the creation of PSOL. During Brazil’s mass demonstrations in June 2013, the party struggled to understand the mobilisation and mostly backed the repression that followed.

    In the next few years, every possible leadership inside and outside the party was neutralised and coopted, and even PSOL ended up becoming nothing more than an appendage of Lula’s party. 

    Limitations of relying on WhatsApp

    The Brazilian experience also raises uncomfortable questions about the growing dependence of progressive politics on personalised leadership and privately controlled digital platforms as WhatsApp channels can disseminate information with extraordinary efficiency, but they cannot, by themselves, replace trade unions, grassroots organisations, political assemblies or the slower, often frustrating process of democratic deliberation.

    A movement of millions that cannot meaningfully question its leadership may be an impressive electoral machine, but it is hardly a democratic revolution, and this is where the lessons for Europe become particularly urgent.

    Progressives in France and Spain are right to seek ways of challenging the far-right’s online influence and they should study Janones’ successes, understand his methods and improve their own digital communication, but they should also recognise that winning an election and building a democratic political movement are fundamentally different objectives.

    Read more

    Two years on, Valencia is still demanding answers for 234 dead in the 2024 flooding – and blaming Sánchez rather than local Popular Party leaders

    The temptation to transform electoral mobilisation into permanent political discipline is particularly dangerous for a left that claims to defend pluralism, collective organisation and popular participation. European progressives should not mistake the ability to command millions of followers for the ability to represent them.

    Ultimately, the greatest danger is not that the left will become identical to the far right by adopting its communication techniques, but rather that in its obsession with defeating the far-right, it may begin treating democratic disagreement as an obstacle rather than a principle worth defending.

    The left cannot defend democracy against the far right by narrowing democratic debate within its own ranks.

    ]]>         Listen: What will it take to make the EU’s next budget work? https://euobserver.com/251763/listen-what-will-it-take-to-make-the-eus-next-budget-work/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 10:14:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251763 European leaders are meeting today with one big issue on the table: how much money the EU should have at its disposal over the next seven years, and where that money should go.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    European leaders are meeting today with one big issue on the table: how much money the EU should have at its disposal over the next seven years, and where that money should go.

    And while we shouldn’t expect a deal just yet, the discussions could give us a clearer picture of where Europe is heading, and who might end up paying for it.

    MFF is the acronym for the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework. The next one will run from 2028 to 2034. If you’ve ever followed the tough negotiations in EU countries over their annual budgets, you can only imagine how difficult it is for 27 countries to agree on a seven-year budget.

    So, today’s and tomorrow’s gathering of EU leaders is just one of many meetings aimed at reaching an agreement on the MFF. This time, the goal is to narrow the gap between the 27 countries and hopefully pave the way for a deal in December.

    Because the question isn’t simply how much money Europe should spend. It’s also about what the EU should prioritise, and how it should pay for it.

    Last Saturday (21 November)), European council president António Costa put forward a new proposal to try to bring countries closer together. Unfortunately, it might not convince everyone just yet.

    Read more

    Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

    Reactions have been mixed. Many governments, particularly in southern and eastern Europe, want to protect existing spending, especially on agriculture and regional development.

    Others want the EU to invest more in industrial development, innovation and competitiveness. And there are also countries that are simply reluctant to see the overall budget increase, or to contribute more money.

    Costa’s proposal tries to strike a balance between these competing demands. He therefore proposes to reduce the overall size of the budget compared with the Commission’s initial proposal, while introducing new sources of revenue for the EU, so that member states don’t have to shoulder the entire financial burden themselves.

    The problem is always: where do you cut? In the latest proposal, the biggest reductions would affect the competitiveness part of the budget. That’s a sensitive issue because European leaders have spent the past few years insisting that Europe needs to invest more in its economy, support businesses and innovation, and compete with the US and China.

    Read more

    [Interview] Europe’s next budget risks ‘making the strong stronger’ by diverting funds from poorer areas, EU regions chief warns

    But at the same time, there are very few areas where governments are willing to cut spending. Agriculture and regional development, for instance, remain particularly sensitive. These are funds that many countries see as essential to supporting farmers, local economies and regions that are struggling economically.

    So, reducing spending on competitiveness may be a way of finding compromises elsewhere. But it also raises questions about whether Europe will have enough money to deliver on its ambitions.

    The parliament is also pushing for a more ambitious budget, arguing that the EU needs more resources to deal with the challenges ahead.

    And that brings us to another part of Costa’s proposal: how to generate more money for the EU.

    One of the options he has put forward is a digital tax. The idea is to introduce a three percent tax on certain large companies operating in Europe. It would apply to companies with an annual global turnover of more than €750m and more than €50m in turnover in the EU from digital activities.

    Read more

    With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter?

    We’re talking mainly about large tech companies. Smaller European firms, such as Mistral AI, would not fall under these thresholds, at least for now. This tax could generate around €5bln a year, or roughly €35bln over the seven-year budget period.

    That would help finance the EU budget without relying entirely on additional contributions from national governments. But getting the 27 countries to agree on a new tax is no easy task.

    Some countries, particularly Ireland, are concerned that taxing large tech companies could make Europe less attractive to investors and encourage businesses to move elsewhere. There are also fears of potential retaliation from the United States.

    Still, this digital tax is one of the options considered most likely to gain support among member states.

    We’ll have to wait, probably a few more weeks, to see whether this tax makes its way into the final agreement.

    ]]>         [Interview] Europe’s next budget risks ‘making the strong stronger’ by diverting funds from poorer areas, EU regions chief warns https://euobserver.com/250658/interview-europes-next-budget-risks-making-the-strong-stronger-by-diverting-funds-from-poorer-areas-eu-regions-chief-warns/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:38:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250658 As 2026 draws to a close, EU institutions and capitals are finalising the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget, with catch-up funding for poor regions likely to face deep cuts, even is its top advocate in Brussels is fighting back. ]]> As the first Hungarian citizen to head an EU institution, Kata Tüttő was predisposed to sympathise with marginalised communities. A former deputy mayor of Budapest, the socialist politician and economist has been heading the European Committee of the Regions since 2025, and now faces the biggest task so far in her role.

    Ahead of a crunch summit at which EU leaders will discuss cuts to the EU budget on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November), Tüttő spoke to EUobserver about the difficulty of getting Brussels to prioritise investment in Europe’s underdeveloped communities.

    What are the risks to the regions under the existing proposals for the 2028-2034 EU budget?

    In the cities and regions, the expectations are big, because we have a lot of challenges. There was a feeling in the air that if we have new strategies, if we have new ambitions to become climate neutral, to become strategically independent, to invest in housing. There was a sense that money will follow.

    One of the most important policies in the European Union is called cohesion policy. Historically, one-third of the budget has gone into food security and common agricultural policy. Now it’s seen as being really justified that we invested, so European farmers don’t stop producing food. The other one-third is the so-called cohesion policy. It’s the most important investment policy of the EU.

    Read more

    Shake-up of EU Commission regions department sparks fears for future of cohesion policy

    So how it works that we have the single market, we make business together in the EU because there’s a free flow of people, capital, services, goods, but the money is not evenly distributed. So the strong are getting stronger, the weak weaker. When the agreement on the single market was born, it was clear that you need a reinvestment policy which somehow connects all of the part of the European territories to the single market. This is cohesion policy. 

    It invests in connecting the territories, connecting the people there, investing in skills, and connecting the businesses to the market. The big change in the architecture of the next budget is that cohesion policy is no longer seen as a standalone European policy, but it is detached from the competitiveness narrative, and is denominated as a national policy.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/27/amazon-sale-deals-deceive-customers-black-friday-cyber-monday</link>
      <description><p>Two-thirds of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale products were priced the same or lower in previous months Groundwork Collaborative finds, a claim Amazon disputes</p><p>An Apple Watch on sale for $680. A pair of women’s Hunter yellow rainboots discounted for $127, and a pair of men’s UGG boots, $180. A Carhartt beanie just shy of $20.</p><p>These discounts – all reportedly featured last year on Amazon’s own curation of its best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals – sound like good deals for the holiday gift season. But a recent analysis from progressive thinktank Groundwork Collaborative found these products and others had been listed at the same price or even less just days before Amazon started advertising them as discounted.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/27/amazon-sale-deals-deceive-customers-black-friday-cyber-monday">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe">Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU</a></p></li></ul><p>Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.</p><p>Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits.       <title>Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses</link>
      <description><p>Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August</p><p>The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/18/abc-sues-trump-federal-communications-commission">sued the agency</a> in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.</p><p>The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/jensen-huang-nvidia-apologizes-staff</link>
      <description><p>Huang acknowledges he violated code of conduct by having affairs, but denied Trump was instrumental in his return</p><p>Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he has caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.</p><p>“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/technology/jensen-huang-apology-nvidia-ceo.html">reviewed by the New York Times</a>. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/jensen-huang-nvidia-apologizes-staff">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age</link>
      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 28 Nov 2026 02:25:51 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[European shares log strong weekly gains as markets await Spanish election]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/european-shares-log-strong-weekly-gains-as-markets-await-spanish-election/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/27/european-shares-log-strong-weekly-gains-as-markets-await-spanish-election/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:26:56 +0000Europe’s benchmark share index closed at a one-week high on Friday after broad sectoral gains, as investors bought riskier assets following steep losses ​earlier this month.

Investors’ attention now turns to Spain’s election on Sunday.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 gained 1 per cent to 643.85 points. It gained nearly 3 per cent on the week, its sharpest weekly rise since mid-May, bouncing back from the steepest weekly decline since late March 2025.

Equities were rebounding from what has been a bruising month for AI-exposed global stocks as investors grew frustrated with returns ‌on ‌debt-backed ​AI investments and a brief leadership crisis at chip giant Nvidia.

Dublin

Shares in Glanbia stabilised somewhat after a rough week, rising by 1 per cent to €17.37.
