]]>xavierarnau<![CDATA[Will the US’s gigantic $3.8tn bet on AI backfire?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/27/will-the-uss-gigantic-38tn-bet-on-ai-backfire/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/27/will-the-uss-gigantic-38tn-bet-on-ai-backfire/Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000By the end of this year the seven biggest artificial intelligence (AI) companies – Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle – will have debt relating to AI investment of $800 billion (€729 billion) sitting on their balance sheets.

Big, yes, but not big enough to call a bubble, and not big enough to trigger a 2008-style crash.

It is the off-balance-sheet debt – now estimated at $3 trillion – that looms like a Manhattan skyscraper over the global financial system.

The Federal Reserve’s latest financial stability report included a section entitled “Leverage in the Data Center Buildout.”

This is the first time the Fed has taken a close look at how the data-centre buildout is being financed.

It noted that while debt balances relating to AI investment have grown (that’s the $800 billion bit), “other obligations” have grown even more rapidly.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

It’s these “other obligations” that are making markets jittery.

The Fed estimates that there is more than $1 trillion in leases signed but not yet commenced, plus more than $2 trillion in what it calls “take-or-pay contracts” and “residual value guarantees” at Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle.

These arrangements let companies with strong credit positions support weaker-credit firms to finance projects “without having an immediate, direct effect on the balance sheets of the stronger-credit firms”.

So, for example, the big firm might agree a long-term lease for data-centre capacity with a third-party data-centre developer which the latter then uses to secure financing to build the data centre. It’s not unlike how a lot of apartment schemes in Ireland are financed.

“The rapid growth of these other obligations represents deepening connections between the largest technology firms and smaller, riskier firms with less access to credit,” the Fed says.

“Via these connections, the largest technology firms may absorb losses in the event of a future downturn, mitigating their effects on the rest of the financial system,” it says.

“However, it also suggests that these firms’ economic exposure to such a downturn may be substantially larger than suggested by their on-balance-sheet liabilities,” it says.

All of which raises the question of who takes the hit if AI demand fails to live up to the hype.

No one is disputing the transformative power of the new technology but the commercialisation of it and the debt racked up to pay for the infrastructure is a different matter.

This is where the comparison with the dot.com bubble of late 1990s comes in. Back then, it seemed like anything with an internet tag was afforded a free run with investors. Price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios were off the charts.

When it came to commercialising the new technology, many firms couldn’t do it or had invested money that didn’t match the potential returns and the investment bubble burst.

The cloud computing, the payment systems, the real value elements of the internet came only later.

The technology at the centre of the dot.com bubble – the internet – went on untrammeled by the boom and bust surrounding it. Many of the companies that built the railways went bust despite the transformative power of rail transport.

Are we on the same arc with AI?

Ireland’s exposure to a potential boom and bust is relatively limited. That’s because the 109 data centres here and those in the pipeline are primarily for cloud computing and streaming services rather than generative AI. Demand for the former is unlikely to decline.

“The material exposure [for Ireland] is more the Irish construction supply chain which is involved in the construction of 70-90 per cent of all data centres in Europe and which supports about 10,000 jobs here,” says Christopher Brown, head of KPMG’s global strategy group in Ireland.

“There is a need [for these firms] to be mindful that there may be a slowdown coming in the European build. It’s not really an Irish build issue any more because the building in Ireland is immaterial,” he says.

The processing power for the large language models has been very conspicuously kept at home in the US to limit China’s access to the computing power needed to develop these advanced AI systems.

Here’s why Irish pension holders should pay attention to the tech sell-off and what is to come

OpenAI’s flagship Stargate data centre campus in Texas covers almost 1,100 acres, equivalent in size to Central Park in New York, and aims to deliver 1.2 gigawatts of power capacity, not far off Ireland’s total data-centre capacity (1.6 gigawatts).

Data-centre developer Nexus has secured $15.6 billion in construction financing to build data centres, across 4,000 acres, in another part of Texas, for Anthropic with Google providing credit support. It will triple Anthropic’s computing capacity.

The US’s data-centre sector is almost 10 times the size of Europe’s with 120 gigawatts of installed capacity versus 14 in Europe.

Next year is increasingly being seen as a potential turning point for AI investment. Some commentators are predicting a major market correction.

The scale of the correction, if it comes, is impossible to predict, but with $3.8 trillion invested, a sharp reversal could have consequences far beyond the technology sector, potentially careering us into another global financial crisis.

As Revolut attracted new Irish users during Covid in 2020, the banks unveiled their plans for Synch.

The company, set up by AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB and the now departed KBC Ireland, started work on its own stand-alone payment app called Yippay.

Within three years, having butted heads with regulators along the way, the banks recognised that the instant payments landscape had changed and Yippay was no more.

The whole plan was not scrapped, however. The technology, provided by Italian paytech company Nexi, was repurposed so that it could be incorporated directly into existing banking apps and Zippay was born.

So how has it been faring and has it helped the banks retain account holders?

“They had to do it,” says Anastasia Turdyeva, Dublin-based director of financial institutions ratings at S&P Global Ratings.

“Almost everyone in Ireland has Revolut – it has been there for years and people have got used to it”. Zippay, she says, “is not yet at full speed” but is well designed and easy to use.

“The volumes are growing. I think in a year’s time it will be more clear if it is on an upward trend,” she says.

The biggest impediment to sustained growth in use of the payment system, says Turdyeva, is that people are accustomed to using Revolut and it enjoys the advantage of being the first to market.

When asked if its members could produce numbers on how many transactions are done using Zippay, the Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) said it was unable to do so.

However, Central Bank of Ireland figures published last month point to a significant change in consumer behaviour, which has been attributed to the new service.

Card spending on financial services fell by more than €600 million, around a third, in August compared to the same month last year.

“This significant decline likely reflects a shift in payment preference rather than reduced consumer spending,” said the Central Bank. “The introduction of account-to-account (A2A) banking services such as Zippay by Irish banks has provided consumers with an alternative payment option.

“Consequently, these transactions are no longer recorded as card payments, explaining the sharp decline in card-based financial services spending.”

Sharon Brennan, head of the BPFI’s collaboration office, said the banks were seeing Zippay usage “grow week on week” and they were currently trying to target a younger cohort across social media platforms.

Zippay needs to play to its natural advantages

“We had a great starting position as the service was made available to all customers of the three banks that had eligible accounts,” she says. “There was no additional registration process for those customers – so we started with a very broad reach from day one.”

Revolut has certainly noticed.

In a meeting with Department of Finance officials in April, its country manager, Malcolm Craig, was reported as saying Zippay gave the traditional banks a “significant competitive advantage”.

However, sources say Craig’s comments were somewhat “throwaway”, and suggest the minutes of the meeting, released under a Freedom of Information request, didn’t represent Revolut’s true position.

“We see [Zippay] as predominantly an alternative – a way for bricks and mortar banks to meet changing customer expectations in the fast-changing world of digital payments,” says Brennan.

“It’s about removing that friction associated with using a traditional Iban [international bank account number] and BIC [bank identifier code]. It removes a huge pain point for customers.”

She says there were a number of regulatory challenges faced by Synch and Yippay that meant the process of bringing a payments service to market took longer – but also the marketplace was changing.

“It just came to a point when everybody had to stand back and look at the way the world was moving,” she says. “We needed to pivot – and that steered us towards going within-app as opposed to offering a stand-alone app”.

Revolut maintains that its transaction volumes have not been impacted since the launch of Zippay – it recently suggested they may have even increased a little since then. A statement in September said the number of peer-to-peer payments “despite the advent of new, direct competition – has continued to rise”.

Lessons from Ireland’s Revolut revolution

The bank says 86 per cent of its Irish customers use the app every month. Revolut does not comment publicly on Zippay.

“It’s tough to know [how widespread use of Zippay is] – it’s a bit of smoke and daggers,” says Darragh Cassidy of the price comparison website Bonkers.ie.

“From an anecdotal point of view, sometimes it is easier to just Zippay someone – you don’t have to top up your app like with Revolut. Now, the user interface isn’t as good – when I send money with PTSB I always feel there is an extra step required.

“When I tell people I’m using Zippay – the reaction is still a little bit ‘What’? I think it is an okay service – a little bit simpler. But for a lot of younger people, who don’t have bank accounts or don’t want one, they are going to be using Revolut constantly.”

It is this generational divide that Revolut will have to now bet on if it wants to crack the truly profitable parts of the Irish market – mortgages and loans. Getting to this point will mean making proper inroads in the current-account market.

I don’t think there is a risk to the established banks from Revolut when it comes to mortgages

Dmitry Nazarov, S&P

Cassidy points to recent figures – such as those contained in a Consumer Sentiment Banking Survey last month – that showed only 6 per cent of Revolut users here identify it as their main account.

“If you ask people: ‘Do you use Revolut?’ And they’ll say, ‘Yes, I do’. Ask them: ‘Do you get paid into your account?’ – and the answer is no. People tend to keep their bank accounts,” he says.

The analysts are very much aware of this.

S&P’s primary credit analyst for Revolut, Dmitry Nazarov, says gaining a higher degree of “primacy” in the Irish current account market is one of the company’s main aims.

“It’s part of a strategy to strengthen and deepen customer relationships across their core markets,” he says. “We see some positive dynamic there – in terms of engagement – but over the past two years the trajectory has been relatively slow.”

The rationale behind capturing a large segment of the deposit market is to provide a foothold that might then enable the digital bank to move into mortgages and personal loans.

Nazarov foresees little real challenge to the traditional banks in the short term.

“Revolut has a very, very small mortgage portfolio,” he says. “It has nothing in Ireland. The mortgage market is quite different in terms of [regulatory] requirements and the infrastructure they will need to build. I think it’s going to be a very long way for them.

“I don’t think there is [a] risk to the established banks from Revolut when it comes to mortgages.”

Against this background, Revolut announced in September that its Irish credit portfolio had surpassed the €1 billion threshold. It said that having achieved that in just over four years underlined the success of its “play for mainstream market share in Ireland” and that almost a tenth of its Irish customer base was borrowing from it.

It’s understood the company is still intent on bringing mortgages to the Irish market and regards them as a priority but there is no clear time line on when this might happen.

As for suggestions that the bank has fallen behind on its overall strategy of growing lending, sources point to recent comments made by Revolut founder Nik Storonsky who said he wanted it to be a bank with “effectively zero risk”.

Storonsky said that while traditional lenders would loan out 100 per cent of their deposits, Revolut would maintain a much lower loan-to-deposit rate.

Revolut’s model, said the Russian-born entrepreneur, was designed to target the most profitable segments of consumer finance – and leave the risky, capital-intensive investment decisions to the older financial institutions.

“Revolut has been very clear that they are going to be selective in their lending business,” says Navarov. “All of the lending growth has been very fast – with the loan portfolio almost doubling every year – but they started from a very low base”.

Turdyeva agrees that there is little imminent threat to the Irish banks from Revolut’s lending plans – but that they need to be aware of what future banking customers, brought up with Revolut and other similar digital banks, will expect in terms of service.

“The fundamentals of the Irish banks are very strong and they have good positioning for a number of years ahead,” says the banking analyst. “What they need to think about is future competition and generational change.

Navro chief Joe Redmond: ‘I don’t quite fit the profile of a fintech start-up CEO at this stage in my career’

“Other services could be considered by Revolut – there are other things where Revolut can be competitive such as investment – it’s still evolving in Ireland.

“Revolut and Monzo are becoming more visible in the space with products other than just payment services. BankInter came into the area a year ago – these guys will also be more active.”

She points to the Government’s Savings and Investment Accounts, which are to be launched next year, as a potential opportunity for Revolut to grow its share of the Irish market. Many users of the Revolut app will be aware that it already enables users to dabble in stock and crypto trading.

“I think this is on the agenda for the domestic banks,” she says. “They are definitely mindful of generational change and preferences. They’ve put a lot of investment into making their apps more appealing. Time will tell – but so far the story is one of being very resilient”.

As for Zippay, it is understood that the Irish banks intend to expand its offering over the coming months. The introduction of QR-code facilities and small-merchant features are thought to be under consideration. This would allow bank customers to use Zippay to quickly buy coffees and other small items.

Sharon Brennan of the BPFI, meanwhile, says Nexi – the provider of Zippay’s software – is “actively engaging” with other Irish financial institutions with a view to rolling it out further.

It’s understood Revolut is not among them – and has no plans on joining. In the meantime, the battle for Irish wallets continues.

Almost 90 per cent of those surveyed acknowledged they had likely rejected real applications in the belief they had been generated by AI and more than half of those employers (49 per cent of the total) suggested they were adding a level of human input at an earlier stage of the process so as to better monitor the AI decisions.

But we humans are not easy to pin down. For one thing, the answer we give to a question often depends on who is asking.

Consider the UK’s long-running Skills and Employment Survey, which has been performed via face-to-face interviews every five years or so since the 1980s in an attempt to trace people’s experiences of work. In 2024, the researchers conducted a parallel survey online to see if the responses would be consistent with the original method. They found evidence of what Francis Green, a University College London emeritus professor who works on the survey, calls “social esteem bias”: respondents were sometimes more positive, or less negative, when asked in person by a fellow human.

The face-to-face method, for example, found that 17 per cent of Britons were dissatisfied with their jobs in 2012, while 14 per cent said the same in 2024. But the web survey responses in 2024 portrayed the workforce in a much grumpier mood: 23 per cent said they were dissatisfied.

This is a potential problem for those who collect data for long time series, many of whom are keen to shift to online survey methods because of rising costs and falling response rates for face-to-face interviews. But an even more profound methodological change is in the offing in certain parts of the research world.

Unlike big surveys with thousands of respondents, qualitative research involves long, in-depth interviews that illuminate some of the nuance and richness of people’s thoughts and experiences (but – due to their cost – on a necessarily small scale). Now, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has opened a new possibility: that chatbots could allow researchers to combine the scale of quantitative data with the richness of qualitative data.

Would we answer questions differently if AI were doing the asking? And if so, how? Nesta, a UK innovation agency, has conducted a series of small, careful experiments with AI in qualitative research over the past few years. At first, they found that AI interviewers solicited short and thin answers from humans. Some respondents even used ChatGPT themselves to look up the “right” answers.

But the technology has advanced since then – in particular, people can now answer via “voice notes” rather than having to type. Mallory Durran, Nesta’s chief technology officer, told me that those who were sceptical about AI still tended to give quite “short or direct” answers, but others found it to be “less judgmental [and] it was actually easier [to share experiences] when you’re not looking into the eyes of another human”.

The other advantage is that people can talk to AI interviewers in whichever language they’re most comfortable in. “Where we’re working with people in a second language, so not in English, you get way more back than we did with face-to-face interviews,” Durran said. “It seems to be really opening the floodgate.”

In other words, AI interviewers might solicit less information from some people, but much more from others. In particular, the technology could allow researchers to gather the experiences of those who have traditionally been hard to reach, particularly because of language barriers. But it won’t solve every old problem (plenty of hard-to-reach people are also digitally disconnected) and will create some new ones.

For my money, the biggest danger will be in the temptation to scale up and up and up. To give an example, Anthropic last year used Claude to interview more than 80,000 people about their AI use across 159 countries in what it called “the largest and most multilingual qualitative study ever conducted”.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

Once AI is gathering so much data, the next temptation – indeed, probably a practical necessity – will be to use it to read and analyse all those interview transcripts too. That could result in a scenario where human researchers don’t conduct the interviews, or even read the answers people give, but instead receive some smooth, machine-processed analysis of what lies beneath. As a result, they would be far less connected to the messy, nuanced complexity of what people had to say. And when it comes to qualitative research, isn’t that the whole point?

It’s a danger that extends beyond this realm, I suspect: we may become so enamoured of our bigger, faster, newly mechanised methods that we forget what we actually wanted to achieve in the first place. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]><![CDATA[Here’s why Irish pension holders should pay attention to the tech sell-off and what is to come]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/26/the-nvidia-saga-and-the-ai-bubble-really-matter-for-your-pension-fund/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/26/the-nvidia-saga-and-the-ai-bubble-really-matter-for-your-pension-fund/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:04:11 +0000Do Irish pension holders need to be worried about the tech sell-off which has hit markets in recent weeks? The Nasdaq index of US shares – largely driven by tech – has lost some 10 per cent and is now up just 1.4 per cent for the year.

The wider S&P500 has lost 8 per cent since its October peak, though is still up nearly 5 per cent since January. Seasoned investors who subscribed for the recent Anthropic flotation and may have holdings on stocks such as Nvidia will, indeed, be biting their nails.

Anthropic shares soared after the recent flotation but at Wednesday’s close were slightly below their $83 (€75.60) float price.

As for Nvidia, who knows what will happen next, though the share surge following the reappointment of Jensen Huang quickly ran out of steam.

But what about ordinary Irish pension fund holders, or perhaps those who have invested cash into exchange-traded funds or other instruments linked to equity markets?

The US has such a big share of world markets that any fund with a share of global equities will be invested here – and this means holding stakes in the big artificial intelligence (AI) players too, given their outsized share of the market. Your pension will in all likelihood have holdings in Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and, before long, Anthropic.

So do investors need to worry about what has happened in recent weeks and what is to come?

A stake in AI

Your pension fund will typically be invested in a range of assets – principally equities, bonds and cash – and in most funds equities will take the largest share. The weightings will typically change over time, with less reliance on equities approaching retirement as a way to lower risk.

So for most pension holders, the big AI players will indeed form part of their portfolio. The fortunes of Jensen Huang and the success of Anthropic’s Claude AI models affect your pension. They have become so dominant in terms of the overall value of markets that this has become inevitable – and the huge gains have given funds a boost over the last few years.

Pension funds vary but Aidan Donnelly, head of global equities at Davy, points out that a pension fund would typically have 55 to 60 per cent invested in equities on average.

The US would typically account for 65 per cent of this index and, to take one example, Nvidia has a market weight of about 6 per cent so it might represent 2-2½ per cent-plus of a typical pension fund.

Figures produced by the pension industry for individual funds confirm this and in some cases the holdings are higher. In the Irish Life Forum 4 fund, for example, a typical mid- to higher-risk product which would be used to build up investment with retirement still a way off, the top 10 equities – all major US companies except for Taiwan Semiconductor – account for 24 per cent of the total fund value.

Five big US firms – Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, account for 18 per cent, with Apple and Nvidia both at about 4.5 per cent. This has paid off this year, with the fund up close to 10 per cent to date despite the recent fall-off in US equities. And the rise in these shares has been stellar over the past few years with Nvidia rising from $50 three years ago to almost $150 now.

But the concentration risk of pension funds to these big players is there, nonetheless. And obviously the risk for those invested outside their pension in US-linked investment funds which match the big indices is all the greater.

The dollar bounce

The US dollar has risen against the euro this year – by close to 7 per cent. This has given a big bounce to Irish pension funds invested in the US when dollar investments are translated back to euro. Donnelly of Davys points out that despite the latest fall-off in US shares from their highs, the annual returns are still generally in double figures in euro terms. In turn this has been a big support to Irish pension funds this year.

The S&P 500 is up by close to 5 per cent from January but add in the impact of the rising US dollar and this brings the total gain in euro terms to about 12 per cent. This gain was 16 per cent in September, but the annual return is still very healthy for investors on this side of the Atlantic. Many Irish pension funds from the main providers are up 10-15 per cent year to date and even more cautious ones are up 7 to 10 per cent.

The AI risk

With funds heavily invested in the AI bubble and the wider US economy which depends on it, it is self-evident that there is a risk if the bubble “bursts”, or even if the more gentle generally downward trend in share prices seen in recent weeks were to continue.

Big international investment houses now publishing their outlooks for 2027 remain broadly upbeat, though conscious of the risks. UBS Securities, for example, says it believes investors should “stay in the market”, though concentrate on diversifying their portfolios in an environment of “elevated uncertainty”.

This uncertainty involves the much-discussed issue of whether the returns from AI will justify investor enthusiasm. With AI investment in the US set to rise, on UBS estimates from $1 trillion in 2026 – the bulk of which comes from the big players – to $1.6 trillion next year, the question is what return this will show and how quickly this will become evident.

If investment continues to outpace returns, investor fears will grow, as we have seen in recent weeks.

This poses a risk for pensions going into 2027. So too does the environment of rising interest rates, which could – if it worsens – lead to falls in the value of bond holdings, another mainstay of pensions. In 2022, both equities and bonds fell together, the nightmare scenario for funds.

But since then returns have been strong and even allowing for 2022 five-year returns for many funds are 20 to 30 per cent.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

The point is that pensions are a longer-term investment and, as Donnelly points out, this means pension holders face volatility but this does not necessarily add up to risk. Someone who has chosen a more aggressive fund and is hoping to buy an annuity may be exposed, but most managed funds will lower risk close to retirement.

And increasingly those taking their pension do so via a vehicle such as an approved retirement fund which means they will remain invested in the market, rather than leaving themselves exposed to the value of their fund on the one day they buy an annuity.

None of this removes the cost of a bursting of the AI bubble – if it happens – to your pension fund which would take time to recoup. It would lead to a painful fall in value. When the dot.com bubble burst in 2000, the S&P 500 dropped 50 per cent in the next two years, as the US fell into recession following the 9/11 attacks and Irish pension funds had two bad years.

There followed a period of strong gains before the 2008 financial crisis. The point is that over the longer term the averages should work in favour of pension investors.

The story of the markets and the US economy in the last few years, as UBS points out, is one of resilience – but nobody knows where the AI story is going.

The State savings scheme

A final thought on the new State savings scheme, due to launch in the middle of next year. The funds which Irish investors will be offered will offer various levels of risk, but the higher-risk ones will be weighted towards equities.

While people understand that their pension funds are longer-term investments, do they realise they need the same mindset for these funds – not that they are saving for retirement, but that equity investing by its nature carries risks and that “needing” the money back at a specific point in, say, a year’s time is a risky strategy?

]]>Eric Luke<![CDATA[Irish housing wealth now close to €1tn]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/irish-housing-wealth-now-close-to-1-trillion/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/irish-housing-wealth-now-close-to-1-trillion/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:59:11 +0000

Irish households now own nearly a €1 trillion worth of property assets, according to the Central Bank.

The regulator’s latest wealth report indicated that housing accounted for 67 per cent – or €956 billion – of the €1.43 trillion in wealth held by households here in the second quarter.

The total net wealth figure represents “a new series high,” the bank said.

It equates to about €245,000 per person, or €724,000 per household.

The wealth of households has risen in tandem with house prices which have doubled in a decade.

The latest quarterly was, however, driven by a rise in financial assets of €35.3 billion, with “positive revaluations” accounting for most of the increase.

Housing wealth increased by €11 billion over the quarter, also due to positive revaluations.

The net wealth of households is calculated by adding the total value of the housing stock and financial assets – such as cash savings, shares, pensions and possessions such as cars and antiques – and subtracting debt owed or liabilities.

It is considered a crude measure of prosperity as it hides the distribution of household assets and liabilities across income groups and age categories.

The latest figures highlight a very uneven distribution of wealth in Ireland, with the total net wealth of households in the poorest half of the distribution accounting for less than 10 per cent (€145 billion) of the national total.

By contrast, the top 10 per cent of Irish households owned €686.7 billion, 47 per cent, of total household net wealth in the State.

“As a result, the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households continued to hold nearly five times the amount held by households in the bottom half of the net wealth distribution all together,” the bank said.

Households in the middle part of the income distribution (deciles six to nine) owned €629.4 billion overall, or 43.1 per cent of total net wealth.

The balance-sheet composition of Irish households also differed significantly depending on the income level.

Households in the top 10 per cent net wealth decile displayed a more diversified portfolio composition with other financial assets (comprising debt securities, listed shares, investment fund shares and life insurance and annuity entitlements) featuring “prominently”, accounting for 19.4 per cent of total assets.

The bank also noted that wealthier households also displayed lower leverage (meaning they had less debt) when compared with households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution.

Conversely, households in the lower deciles held their financial wealth mainly in deposits (18.5 per cent of their total assets) and were significantly more leveraged (28.1 per cent).

Ella Gleeson, private client manager with wealth advisers NFP Ireland, said: “While today’s report shows that household wealth continues to rise in Ireland, increasing by almost €43 billion, rising living costs are putting pressure on disposable incomes and could make it harder for families to save, invest and build their wealth.

“Today’s report shows that a significant proportion of Irish household wealth is tied up in property,” she added. “While rising property values can make families wealthier on paper, that does not necessarily mean they have greater financial resilience.”

]]>Daragh Mc Sweeney/Provision<![CDATA[High Court refuses to approve Bawag deal to buy PTSB ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/high-court-refuses-to-approve-bawag-deal-to-buy-ptsb/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/high-court-refuses-to-approve-bawag-deal-to-buy-ptsb/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:50:20 +0000The High Court in Dublin has refused to approve Austrian banking group Bawag’s planned €1.62 billion takeover of PTSB because a separate vote of minority shareholders had not been carried out.

The transaction was structured as a so-called scheme of arrangement that required court approval.

The decision, which came as a surprise to Bawag and PTSB, leaves them weighing a number of options. They could appeal the decision; PTSB could call another extraordinary general meeting (EGM) to put the deal before minority investors; or Bawag could change the structure of the deal to a straightforward tender offer to shareholders, which could give it a majority, but not 100 per cent control.

A 4.4 per cent surge in PTSB shares to €3.10 a share, 13 cents above Bawag’s offer, suggests some investors see the Austrian bank having to improve its bid to win over minorities, or another suitor emerging.

PTSB and Bawag each released short statements saying they were considering the judgment and would make further announcements “in due course”.

Skoczylas, managing director of Malta-based Scotchstone Capital, has pursued a number of cases through the Irish courts since the State took control of PTSB in 2011 amid a €4 billion bailout as the bank’s bad loan losses soared after the 2008 financial crash.

“One of the well-developed principles to guard against an unfair or oppressive result is the requirement in certain cases to divide the members or creditors voting on a scheme into separate classes,” Quinn said.

“In those cases the scheme must be approved by a special majority in each class. An unfairness would arise if a scheme is approved by a majority whose legal rights differ, or whose legal position may benefit from the scheme differently, from the minority on whom the scheme is to be imposed.”

The judge said in this case the non-Minister shareholders were entitled to a separate vote.

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[‘Your network is your net worth’: The lessons of a young medtech founder]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/25/your-network-is-your-net-worth-the-lessons-of-a-young-medtech-founder/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/25/your-network-is-your-net-worth-the-lessons-of-a-young-medtech-founder/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:55:00 +0000Building a business is as much about who you know as what you know, according to Max Crinion-Morgan, a young medtech entrepreneur who put his nursing degree on hold to develop a device for monitoring patients’ respiratory rates.

Speaking to an audience of entrepreneurs who featured in The Irish Times Innovators to Watch series over the last 12 months, Crinion-Morgan said “your network is your net worth” and building his network was essential to getting his company off the ground.

“Starting out as a student, I had zero network. But with every single person I talked to, I usually aim to get three contacts from them,” he said.

It didn’t come naturally to him. “I’m one of the most introverted people out there,” he said. “The cold calls are brutal.”

But Crinion-Morgan said the perseverance needed to be driven by something deeper than financial rewards or a desire for autonomy.

He recalled being told he was “crazy” to put his nursing degree on hold and that he needed more experience before starting a business.

“Yes, I don’t have experience, but I am young and I have no responsibilities, and therefore this is one of the greatest times ever just to throw yourself in a direction.”

For him, the motivation to make RespÉire a success is intensely personal. His uncle died in circumstances that left him questioning whether more effective respiratory monitoring might have made a difference.

More recently his father had a heart attack and underwent emergency open-heart surgery. After his father was transferred from intensive care to a general ward, Crinion-Morgan said he pushed for his respiratory rate to be checked. A serious chest infection was subsequently identified and his father returned to intensive care.

“This can be very difficult to do due to the constant disruptions that are commonplace on wards. RespÉire aims to solve the problem by providing a portable, inexpensive and simple-to-use measuring device that aligns with current clinical workflows.”

The idea is that the R3, which is small and light, would find a home on the observation trolley alongside other vital-sign-measuring equipment. It is a plug-and-play device with a screen that displays the reading. The R3 is non-invasive and attaches to the patient’s clothing. It takes between 60 and 80 seconds to take a measurement.

He said his family experiences reinforced his belief that founders need a mission capable of carrying them through the difficult times of getting a business off the ground.

He said there would be days where you think to yourself “I don’t want to do this. I don’t want to have that conversation. I don’t want to take that flight.”

]]><![CDATA[Tech sector is trapped by its own cult of personality]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/tech-sector-is-trapped-by-its-own-cult-of-personality/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/tech-sector-is-trapped-by-its-own-cult-of-personality/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Look in my eyes, what do you see? Thus Corey Glover begins Living Colour’s 1988 classic Cult of Personality. The opening guitar riff drags your attention from whatever you are doing and demands your focus.

The song dives into the faith that ordinary people are willing to put into charismatic individuals, irrespective of ideology or moral stance. It was partially inspired by Khrushchev denouncing Stalin in 1956, but also makes reference to Gandhi and JFK.

In related news, Jensen Huang is back as chief executive of Nvidia after being out of his job just long enough to finish GTA VI.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, has returned to the job after an extraordinary fortnight. His resignation on November 12th followed revelations about extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The other allegations related to staff members of Nvidia.

These are normal reasons to resign or be ousted. That goes for the vast majority of people in leadership positions in companies of all sizes globally, let alone the boss of a company upon which the artificial intelligence (AI) sector is dependent.

Almost immediately, calls came for Huang to be reinstated. Elon Musk and Donald Trump were among the loudest advocates. On November 17th, Nvidia’s board said he would not be reinstated. By Monday, November 23rd, that had all changed and he was back in the top job.

The market loved the news, Nvidia’s share price rose by 31.5 per cent on Monday after plummeting in the week and a half following his resignation. While the price has bounced back, it is still considerably down on when news of Huang’s indiscretions were first revealed.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

That the price can swing so wildly based on the whims and actions of one man is not healthy. Huang is one of a long line of tech leaders who have been elevated in importance above the institution they lead.

In simple terms, Jensen Huang has become an existential necessity for Nvidia.

It’s somewhat apt that at a time of discussions about AI replacing humans in more and more facets of work and life, that the boss of the most important AI company is deemed irreplaceable.

Automation is meant to be capable of replacing quite a lot of the duties in management and tech roles, yet this tech company can’t manage without a 63-year-old that loves his leather jacket.

We’re far beyond debates of right and wrong or what is fair. This is a matter of an industry making itself needlessly fragile.

Think of the corporate governance implications of this. The board of Nvidia has essentially shown itself to be incapable of keeping out an individual who is a walking example of someone that should be kept as far away from the business as possible.

Even allowing for the pressure that can be exerted by the US president, this fixation on a single figure is a recipe for disaster across the sector.

US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks

That Huang’s initial departure could cause such a mighty downward swing in Nvidia’s stock should alarm the whole industry. The partial, but far from total, rebound upon his return is just as concerning.

Moving on from a founder boss isn’t easy, yet it can be done. Apple took the mildest of early hits to its share price when Tim Cook replaced Steve Jobs, granted that was the second run of Jobs in the top job. Microsoft’s share price actually went up notably after Steve Ballmer replaced Bill Gates.

Donald Trump proposes raft of new tariffs on major economies

Yet those were planned continuity switches. The plan for Nvidia seems to be to trust that Huang will live forever.

It’s far from alone. Mark Zuckerberg is essentially unsackable at Meta, Elon Musk is in similar if not quite so invulnerable a position at both Tesla and SpaceX.

In the case of either having to depart due to unforeseen circumstances, who steps in as the boss is far from obvious. We’ve already seen this when Sam Altman had to essentially be his own replacement at OpenAI in 2023 as his dismissal by the board led to a revolt from staff.

That goes across the board in the sector as it currently stands. It doesn’t have to be this way, Uber survived the sudden and explosive departure of Travis Kalanick. Bill McDermott’s departure at SAP was in no way controversial but it was extremely sudden, yet SAP still managed fine.

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang apologises to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’

Now, more than ever, the tech sector is trapped by its own cult of personality. Investment has always been about people more than products, but the Jensen Huang situation has taken this to extremes.

A cult of personality isn’t just about the person being worshipped but about the people willing to do the worshipping.

The market is at a point where it doesn’t trust multitrillion dollar companies with tens of thousands of highly skilled employees to function without the one true leader.

Vibes and pixie dust seem to be the foundations of the industry as it stands.

Seeking permission to live here through study and employment permits are now his best option, says McLaughlin.

To get a student visa as a non-European Economic Area (EEA) national in Ireland, you must get admission to a full-time course listed on the Government-maintained Interim List of Eligible Programmes. Accounts filed for Sherry FitzGerald Group Ireland Holdings Ltd show it sold 10,500 residential units, which included sales in Northern Ireland, with a total value of €5.1 billion.

In the Republic Sherry FitzGerald sold 8,900 units (up 100 year on year) between its own network and franchisees. These units had a capital value of €4.5 billion, or an average price of €505,617 (up from an average of €488,636 a year earlier).

The group employs 600 people across 114 offices comprising 35 owned-business offices and 74 franchise offices in the Republic. It also has five offices in Northern Ireland through its Simon Brien subsidiary, which was acquired in January 2024.

In February this year it completed the acquisition of rival HT Meagher O’Reilly, which trades as Knight Frank Ireland.

The latest accounts show operating profit rose to €1.3 million in 2025, up from €500,000, while the company’s cash position was €9.6 million, up from €7.7 million in 2024.

No dividend was paid to its owner, Tommy Kelly’s CastleGate Investments, last year. In 2024 it paid a dividend of €6 million.

The company sold 4,500 properties through its owned-business network last year with a capital value of €2.8 billion.

Directors noted that the main risks to the group were “a local or global economic downturn due to the current macroeconomic environment, which continues to create uncertainty, particularly over the level of demand for the group’s services”.

Other risks included “unexpected events such as global geopolitical uncertainty, unforeseen changes in consumer sentiment, planning and regulatory restrictions that negatively impact new development and funding constraints,” they said.

While property price inflation has slowed in recent months due to higher borrowing costs and elevated inflation, property values are still appreciating.

“The financial performance of the group was underpinned by a stable property market,” chief executive Marian Finnegan said.

“In Ireland, housing completions increased by more than 20 per cent to reach 36,246 and average property values rose by almost 7 per cent,” she said.

“That said, supply is still falling well short of demand, which underpins the upward pressure on prices,” Finnegan said.

“Looking ahead, we expect demand for quality homes to remain resilient across the island, while supply constraints are likely to persist,” she said.

The supply of new homes is expected to hit 40,000 this year but to remain below the Government’s target level of 50,000 in 2027 and 2028.

Finnegan noted that Sherry Fitzgerald’s Northern Ireland business “performed well” supported by a strong economy.

Residential sales in the North reached 24,667 in 2025, the highest level since 2022.

“New home completions stood at 5,844 in 2025, reflecting a tight supply environment,” she said.

]]><![CDATA[US comedy gag about a sister who quits job to care for dad is no joke]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000

If you didn’t laugh, you may have cried – or maybe you did both – after watching Saturday Night Live’s Sister sketch when it flooded into family and friends’ messaging apps earlier this month.

In the American comedy programme’s skit, a son realises his ageing father needs more care at home but he doesn’t want to put Dad in a nursing home and live-in care could cost thousands.

He says: “I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live-in 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free and also … your sister.

“Signing up couldn’t be easier. Simply text ‘Dad fell’ to Sister and she will quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him.”

She manages medications, handles doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, and can even bring her reluctant husband along – all without affecting the son’s 50 per cent share of the inheritance – because the parents’ will predates their dementia. Now, the son says, “I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

The parody ends with “Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has a good therapist.”

The comedy lands so well because it’s painfully true. “When care intensifies, women’s employment pays the price,” according to the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). When care is unavailable, unaffordable or does not meet families’ needs, someone has to fill the gap. Too often, that someone is a woman.

“What may begin as a private decision about how a family organises care can therefore have very broad consequences for employment, income and gender equality,” says EIGE.

Of course, plenty of men look after their parents and children, too. But as care responsibilities intensify over time, it’s women who are substantially more likely than men to leave employment. Lower-income carers, who tend to be women, are most exposed to care-related employment penalties. EIGE says “27 per cent of lower-income carers report reducing working hours or leaving employment due to care, compared with 20 per cent of middle-income carers and 17 per cent of higher-income carers”.

The big squeeze

With an estimated one in nine people in the workforce both caring for a loved one and managing their career, employers need to start future-proofing their employee benefits. The numbers are probably going only one way due to our ageing population but supports, both private and public, are limited.

In Ireland, employer-funded carer supports fall into two main categories: dedicated paid carer leave, which is still rare, and structured, carer-friendly workplace programmes. which are unpaid and more common in large employers.

The State offers limited supports for carers. Under the Carer’s Leave Act, eligible employees can take unpaid leave of between 13 and 104 weeks to provide full-time care to a qualifying person. Employees may qualify for Department of Social Protection payments such as carer’s benefit (PRSI-based) or carer’s allowance (means-tested). There’s also statutory medical care leave of up to five days of unpaid leave in a 12-month period.

Family Carers Ireland (FCI) estimates there are more than 624,000 family carers, and that at least 270,000 are balancing paid work with care. FCI thinks the number of working carers is even higher than that, as many people do not see themselves as carers. They see themselves simply as wives, daughter, sons or neighbours.

When South East Technological University surveyed its staff after joining FCI’s Caring Employers programme, 60 per cent identified as family carers. Most employers simply never ask this question, so the numbers are hard to quantify.

Ibec’s Better Care Better Business report, published in March 2024, gives us a snapshot of what this costs carers who also work outside the home. Of the carers surveyed, 63 per cent were in employment and 73 per cent of those found it challenging to balance work and care. Some 57 per cent reported added financial pressure and more than a third said caring had affected their careers.

Carers are often exhausted and don’t know where to turn for support. While 57 per cent said their employer had been flexible, only 29 per cent were aware of a company policy on caring and just 21 per cent had ever received paid leave for it. Most support seems to depend on company or managerial goodwill.

‘I care for my elderly parents, but my efforts are taken for granted. I think I might be going mad’

FCI’s State of Caring 2026 report, based on responses from 2,930 carers, describes the reality of informal unpaid supports. Some 71 per cent say caring has harmed their health, and the same proportion find it difficult to make ends meet.

When caring responsibilities become unmanageable, employees are often forced to make difficult choices. Some reduce their hours, others take extended leave and many leave the workforce altogether, often permanently. Carers who remain in work report less loneliness than those who have left, which is one reason the charity wants carers kept in employment wherever possible.

Amongst women: Why are there so few men in caring roles?

The cost to employers in recruitment, training and lost institutional knowledge is significant, and it is largely avoidable. Unaddressed caregiving interruptions carry real costs, including an estimated €615 million annually in Ireland from eldercare-related work disruptions alone, says FCI.

Small, practical actions can make a meaningful difference to employees such as offering flexible working options, showing understanding during challenging periods, encouraging open and respectful conversations, providing access to leave and wellbeing supports, communicating information on rights and entitlements through human resources and fostering empathetic leadership.

‘All the caring I put into my parents – the time, effort and money – is gone, wasted’

Employer toolkit

  1. Find out who your carers are. Run an anonymous survey. Most will not volunteer the information and many do not use the word carer.
  2. Write a carer policy and publicise it. If only three in 10 carers know a policy exists, it’s not doing its job.
  3. Train line managers. When flexibility is granted informally, it’s only as good as the next manager.
  4. Offer to pay for some carer days beyond the legal requirement, and ensure that dependents include parents, in-laws and other relatives. Family comes in many shapes and sizes.
  5. Make flexibility two-way. Offer workers compressed or reduced hours with an agreed route back to full hours when care needs change.
  6. Introduce a carer passport so arrangements do not have to be renegotiated after every restructure or new manager.
  7. Provide practical information. In the middle of a crisis, most people first need to understand home supports, the Fair Deal scheme and enduring power of attorney. The local HSE home support office or public health nurse is often the first port of call.
  8. Plan for the carers you will have. With an ageing population, employees who are not carers today will be tomorrow so explore those pathways now.

So, what’s the real cost of the Sister gag? The punchline is that Sister is free. She’s not. The cost shows up in her health, her hours, her reduced pension pot and her lost promotion prospects. Eventually it shows up for her employer too, in turnover and lost experience, when she decides the only way to manage is to leave.

Employers can’t make relatives share the load. But they can stop assuming that someone’s sister – who might also be their best employee – will absorb it.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

]]>FredFroese<![CDATA[Medtech start-up wants to take the guesswork out of blood pressure readings]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/medtech-start-up-wants-to-take-the-guesswork-out-of-blood-pressure-readings/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/medtech-start-up-wants-to-take-the-guesswork-out-of-blood-pressure-readings/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 03:15:00 +0000White coat syndrome describes the spike in blood pressure (BP) experienced by one in five adults when it is taken in a medical setting.

It’s a problematic syndrome because those with otherwise normal pressure can end up taking medication they don’t need, while those already on medication may be put on a higher dose than is necessary.

Compounding the problem is the fact that most practitioners don’t have the time during a consultation to follow measurement protocols that recommend a patient sit in silence for five minutes to become calm before their blood pressure reading is taken.

In short, the traditional method of taking BP is flawed, and it was this shortcoming that prompted medtech start-up Wavescope to develop a technology that can assess when someone is physiologically ready to have their blood pressure taken. Readings taken at this point are significantly more accurate.

“No other technology assesses when a person is in the correct physiological state,” says Wavescope founder and chief executive Seán McMahon. “Our nearest competitor assesses physiological state during measurement, which gives rise to (other) problems. Our technology offers significant advantages, akin to walking versus flying, if fast travel is preferred.

“The under and overtreatment of hypertension is a really big health issue,” McMahon adds. “The figures for white coat hypertension rise as high as 40 per cent for people already diagnosed with blood pressure problems, and unreliable blood pressure readings can result in misdiagnosis, mistreatment, medical harm and even death.”

Wavescope was set up in 2023, and its patent-pending technology works off a proprietary algorithm that continuously reads a patient’s electrical bio-signals to determine when they are relaxed.

This is done via the ECG (electrocardiogram) or PPG (photoplethysmography) measurements the device is already taking.

The ECG tests heart rhythm and electrical activity, while PPG measures volumetric changes in blood circulation at the skin’s surface. Once the patient’s vital signs have settled, and this will vary from person to person, the system triggers the cuff to inflate.

“The aim is to take a patient’s blood pressure at the optimum time, not as soon as they walk through the door, which is what usually happens. This is a huge change in the way blood pressure is measured. We call it the reliability shift,” McMahon says.

“Wavescope works with the signals already inside monitors and wearables, so no new hardware is required. We license our ‘readiness layer’ as a component or software on silicon, and it is designed for OEM [original equipment manufacturer] integration. It is not a stand-alone medical device,” adds McMahon, an electronic engineer by background whose co-founders are commercial director Steen Gordon, chief commercial officer Alan Gormley and Dr Jennifer Grant, clinical lead at Beacon HealthCheck who deals with the problems of unreliable BP monitoring devices in her clinics every day.

“The research shows that over 70 per cent of physicians, over 90 per cent of nurses and technicians and over 90 per cent of adults taking their blood pressure at home measure without any waiting time,” McMahon says.

“The guidelines now are to wait five minutes. In the 1960s the recommended wait period was 45 minutes. Measuring blood pressure before a patient has settled can lead to variability and a shift in readings by 10mmHg or more. That is enough to complicate clinical assessment, and as things stand, the diagnosis follows the number.”

McMahon is no stranger to new product development, having spent his career in the tech sector in various roles, including principal design engineer and chief technology officer. In 2018, he cofounded mdci.io, which developed and deployed a hospital diabetes administration system and built an artificial intelligence neural network model for diabetic retinopathy grading.

McMahon already has a postgraduate degree in engineering, but in 2021, with Covid in full swing, he decided to use the time to add to his qualifications with a master’s degree in advanced medical technology. It was during this time that the concept for what has since developed into Wavescope’s technology first surfaced following McMahon’s research into blood pressure error mitigation around wait times.

A subsequent pilot study conducted with UCD and Centric Healthcare in 2024 confirmed the reliability problem with existing measurement methods, and things have since moved on to the point where the company is now preparing for two big clinical trials. Its technology is due for commercial launch in 2028 and will go to market under the name BP VeraState.

“Our first market will be the US via FDA [food and drug administration] approval, as the speed to approval is significantly faster. Our technology will offer blood pressure monitor original equipment manufacturers a huge competitive advantage,” says McMahon, whose company has teamed up with Taiwan-based medical device manufacturer Health & Life (blood pressure monitor specialists) as its primary partner.

Innovation: All you need to know

“Once devices with Wavescope hit the market, we expect our technology to ripple quickly throughout the sector of approximately 90 million units per annum,” he adds. “Globally, an estimated 1.4 billion adults aged 30–79 years worldwide had hypertension in 2024. This represents 33 per cent of the population in this age range.”

Enterprise Ireland has backed Wavescope with pre-seed start funding of €100,000, while in 2024 the company joined a UCD-led disruptive technologies consortium and secured €1 million in support from the State-backed disruptive technologies innovation fund.

Wavescope, which is Dublin-based and employs four, is now looking to raise a further €1.25 million to unlock the disruptive technologies award, complete its clinical investigations in conjunction with University College Dublin and St Vincent’s hospital and to gather the necessary data for FDA approval for its measurement technology.

“We’ve been incredibly fortunate with the help we’ve had from companies such as Microchip Technology and Analog Devices in building our reference prototype device,” McMahon says.

“We’ve also pulled together a highly experienced team of advisers, including Prof Brian Caufield [an expert in leveraging data from wearables and mobile sensing]. We have had good support from Enterprise Ireland, UCD and Irish Manufacturing Research, but in terms of funding there is a very big gap between the commercialisation fund and the pre-seed start fund. An intermediary scheme might help support more entrepreneurs who cannot afford to wait or afford to forgo a salary,” McMahon says.

   <title>Deutlich zu warmer und zu trockener Herbst</title>
   <description>Der Herbst hat heuer am Ende zwar einen kräftigen Wintereinbruch gebracht, über weite Strecken waren die Temperaturen in den letzten Wochen aber überdurchschnittlich. Damit gehört der Herbst 2026 zu den wärmsten fünf Prozent seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen 1767. Zudem war er überdurchschnittlich sonnig und deutlich zu trocken mit enormen Witterungsschwankungen: Von Hochsommerhitze bis zu Schnee und Dauerfrost war alles dabei.</description>

Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Fri, 27 Nov 2026 21:13:19 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 President vetoes Polish government’s middle-class tax cuts https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/27/president-vetoes-polish-governments-middle-class-tax-cuts/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 21:02:06 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107596

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill that would have lowered income tax for millions of people earning around or slightly above average salaries, while increasing taxes on large companies and the highest earners.

Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the income-tax cut would benefit only a small minority of workers, while the changes to corporate taxes would disproportionately affect Polish businesses, as international corporations could move profits abroad.

The government, however, rejected Nawrocki’s reasoning, accusing the president of siding with large corporations at the expense of ordinary working Poles.

❌ Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o reformie podatkowej. pic.twitter.com/tvXCVKnTMs

— Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 27, 2026

The legislation, which was due to come into force in 2027 – an election year – would have adjusted the income tax brackets, including an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets.

Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €26,850) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%.

There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount.

Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%.

 

According to the government’s estimates, 3.5 million workers would benefit from the reform. However, Nawrocki said that this means around nine out of every ten taxpayers would not benefit. He also claimed that in practice the reform

“This bill divides citizens. It gives to a few, while taking away from the majority,” said Nawrocki in a video published on social media.

The president also noted that the government had failed to deliver on its promise, made when coming to power in 2023, to double the tax-free income allowance to 60,000 zloty, a change that would have benefited a much broader group of taxpayers, including the lowest earners.

According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,405.19 zloty in October this year, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year.

The Polish government has approved a final version of the state budget for 2027, including planned middle-class tax cuts funded by higher rates on the richest.

The budget act and associated legislation still need approval from parliament and the president https://t.co/I2Gz0h6cHd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 29, 2026

To finance the proposed relief, the legislation also included an increase in the corporate income tax (CIT) rate from 19% to 22% for companies and tax groups generating annual revenues above €50 million.

The solidarity levy paid by highest-earners would have also increased to 5%, while the earnings limit for qualifying for a simplified lump-sum tax on gross business revenue – commonly used by professionals such as lawyers, IT specialists and healthcare workers – would be lowered from €2 million a year to €250,000.

Nawrocki criticised the government for making the “entry into force of the tax relief contingent upon the simultaneous implementation of tax hikes.” He said that the higher corporate tax would disproportionately fall on “Polish, growing firms,” while “foreign ones will move their profits to other countries”.

Credit rating agency S&P has revised Poland’s outlook to negative.

It notes that the country has seen "one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally", while "political polarisation" and "institutional tensions" make consolidation unlikely https://t.co/2Nix7R6Pjj

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 7, 2026

Finance minister Andrzej Domański condemned Nawrocki’s veto, saying that he had taken “the side of large corporations rather than the Polish people”.

“Only the Grinch and the Nawrocki can steal people’s money right before Christmas,” wrote Prime Minister Donald Tusk on social media.

However, Nawrocki’s veto was welcomed by the right-wing opposition. Sławomir Mentzen, a leader of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), praised the president for blocking what he described as “another government attempt to harm Polish businesses”.

Mariusz Błaszczak, a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice, said that his party wanted to raise the second income tax thresshold from 120,000 to 180,000 zloty, but “without introducing any hidden tax increases”.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

📽️ Regardez la vidéo explicative sur les affaires de Grande Chambre sur l'instrumentalisation de la migration. pic.twitter.com/ZhXqZ6lIur

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

 

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had  “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus https://t.co/7Gbsvs6I1e

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

A court has found that Poland's border guard violated the law when sending two Afghan and Ethiopian men back to Belarus after they injured themselves crossing the anti-migrant border fence.

One of them had made clear his wish to claim asylum in Poland https://t.co/42yOuGEgns

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2024

For Poland, the case concerned an unnamed Afghan national who had been part of a group that had crossed back and forth over the Polish-Belarusian border multiple times, as often happened in the early stages of the crisis.

The ECHR noted that it had, at the time, issued an interim measure requiring that the Afghan man not be returned to Belarus.

However, the Polish authorities did not take this into account, and sent him back to Belarus on 20 October 2021, thereby demonstrating they had not complied with their obligation to properly assess his need for protection, found the ECHR.

The court also ruled that, in the case of that applicant as well as a fellow Afghan national, Poland had violated their rights by preventing lawyers from having access to them. It ordered Poland to pay the two men €20,000 (89,000 zloty) and €5,000 respectively as compensation.

Two Afghan asylum seekers who crossed from Belarus into Poland have been awarded compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

They were detained and driven back towards the border by officers, who did not accept their asylum applications https://t.co/M9bSHakS5j

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2025

In Latvia’s case, the ECHR ruled that the country had violated its obligations by sending Iraqi Kurdish children, some of whom were infants, back into Belarus, “disregarding the[ir] evident vulnerability”.

At the same time, the European court dismissed further complaints by adult migrants against Latvia and Lithuania, finding that they had not demonstrated any vulnerability or risk.

However, it did find that Lithuania had violated some Cuban migrants’ rights by failing to properly inform them of the reasons they were being held in a detention camp and thereby also of their right to legally challenge their detention.

It also ruled that Latvia had violated the rights of migrants on its territory due to the poor conditions they found themselves in when camped out on Latvian territory, with no access to sanitary facilities and insufficient protection from rain and cold nighttime temperatures.

⚖️ Grand Chamber cases

➡️ Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, European Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections.

🔗 Press release: https://t.co/nflEyCWKb1

— ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 24, 2026

In response to today’s ruling on Poland, the deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy, Maciej Duszczyk, hailed it as “very important and favourable for us”.

He said that the ECHR’s findings regarding states’ rights to defend their borders from instrumentalised migration effectively endorsed Poland’s policies.

The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a Warsaw-based NGO, also noted that the ECHR’s Grand Chamber had, for the first time, defined the scope of states’ obligations when another state has instrumentalised migration.

“In the ECHR’s view, when migration is instrumentalised, states are not obliged to assess whether people being returned to the state instrumentalising migration will have access to an adequate asylum procedure there,” noted HFPC.

Bardzo ważny i dobry dla nas wyrok Europejskiego Trybunału Praw Człowieka.
Niezakwestionowano naszego modelu walki z nielegalną migracją.
Trybunał odniósł się do instrumentalizacji jako sprzecznej z Konwencją i podkreślił prawo państ do obrony i ochrony swoich granic.

— Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) November 24, 2026

A number of Polish courts have also found that the authorities violated the rights of migrants on the Belarus border. Last year, two Afghan asylum seekers were awarded 5,000 zloty compensation for their mistreatment by Polish border guards.

In 2024, another court found that the border guard violated the law when sending Afghan and Ethiopian migrants back to Belarus after they had injured themselves while crossing the border.

Last year, Poland’s government effectively formalised pushbacks by introducing a ban on asylum claims by people crossing the border irregularly from Belarus, who are now sent back without their applications being accepted.

The measure has been criticised by human rights groups – including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Poland’s own human rights commissioner – as a violation of international law and Poland’s constitution.

The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%

Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026

Poland has also implemented a number of other tough policies, including easing rules for the use of firearms by uniformed officers protecting the border from illegal migration.

This year has seen the migration crisis abate significantly, with Poland reporting a 98% decline in attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, as well as a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do cross.
