City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 27 Nov 2026 20:26:21 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Lloyds emerges as frontrunner to buy Aldermore https://www.cityam.com/lloyds-emerges-as-frontrunner-to-buy-aldermore/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:45:12 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2484133

Lloyds has emerged as the frontrunner to buy alternative lender Aldermore after rival bidders dropped out or excluded the group’s motor finance division from their bids, City AM has learned. The FTSE 100 bank is now in pole position to buy the entire Aldermore group, in a sale that would include both its bank and [...]]]>

Lloyds has emerged as the frontrunner to buy alternative lender Aldermore after rival bidders dropped out or excluded the group’s motor finance division from their bids, City AM has learned.

The FTSE 100 bank is now in pole position to buy the entire Aldermore group, in a sale that would include both its bank and car finance lender, Motonovo, sources said.

South African lender Firstrand put Aldermore up for sale in April this year and received initial interest from around a dozen suitors.

The process has been narrowed down to its last few bidders, which are seeking to buy either parts of or the entirety of the bank. Analysts at RBC said they expect the group to fetch a price tag of between £1.1bn and £1.6bn.

Investec, which is dual-headquartered in the UK and South Africa, is among the final contenders circling the banking unit but is keen to avoid Motonovo, the group’s loss-making motor finance lender, sources said. Private equity firms Warburg Pincus and Cerberus had also submitted a joint bid for the company but have since pulled back from the deal.

Firstrand is leaning towards selling the group collectively in a single deal to Lloyds, the sources said. They cautioned that no deal has been finalised and the situation could yet change.

Lloyds, Investec and Aldermore declined to comment.

Motor finance woes follow Aldermore

Motonovo is understood to have been a source of friction for some bidders. The car finance market has been in turmoil after the City watchdog set out a multi-billion pound compensation scheme earlier this year over historic missold loans.

Motonovo recognised a £153.2m charge in its latest accounts to pay for the redress scheme. This was more than double the £60.6m recorded the prior year.

The Supreme Court partially overturned a landmark ruling on car finance deals last year, rejecting claims that hidden commissions were automatically unlawful. But it found one customer’s undisclosed commission created an “unfair relationship”, leaving the door open for an industry-wide payout.

Firstrand confirmed it was selling Aldermore after voicing frustration at the Financial Conduct Authority’s compensation scheme. 

Lloyds owns the UK’s largest motor finance lender and has provisioned some £2bn for the ongoing mis-selling scandal.

A tie-up with Aldermore would allow the blue-chip banking group to beef up its standing in buy-to-let (BTL) mortgages, where it currently dominates 15 per cent of the market through its subsidiary BM Solutions.

Some 40 per cent of Aldermore’s £17bn loanbook also comes from the BTL market.

]]> 2484133 Charlie Conchie Charlie Conchie Game on: How to make the most of game season https://www.cityam.com/game-on-how-to-make-the-most-of-game-season/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:32:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2484149

Game season is well and truly underway across the UK. As cooks’ minds start to wander towards the turkey and goose, spare a thought for the partridge. Game has a bad rep: too metallic, too lean, too hard to cook. Growing up my mum – too embarrassed to turn down his gamey advances – used [...]]]>

Game season is well and truly underway across the UK. As cooks’ minds start to wander towards the turkey and goose, spare a thought for the partridge. Game has a bad rep: too metallic, too lean, too hard to cook. Growing up my mum – too embarrassed to turn down his gamey advances – used to take pheasants that were gifted to us by an eccentric local. She would try to disguise in chicken pies and curries, but we always knew. Teeth would crunch down in metal shotgun pellets and it tasted terrible. But when done well, it can steal the show. No wonder restaurants are stuffing their menus with squabs and grouse. 

Tomás Gormley, chef-owner of Cardinal in Edinburgh says: “Every year I do a partridge and bread sauce dish, usually with some sort of stone fruit. This year we’re getting some amazing damsons, so I’ll definitely incorporate them into that somewhere.

“I’m also growing some fantastic spaghetti squash and radicchio in our kitchen garden, so I’m excited about pairing those with game. I cook all the game we get at Cardinal over coals on the barbecue. I usually rest it in a tray of seasoned duck fat to keep it moist while cooking it slowly over the heat. Game is usually quite lean, so you need to be very careful when cooking it. Getting it right really pays off, though.”

Cooking royalty and Irish bon vivant Richard Corrigan’s partridge in a pear tree dish is an ideal as we shift into December. The gaminess of the bird works perfectly with fruit and warming ginger.

Spatchcock partridge with pears, quince and lentils

Partridges

  • 2 partridges

For the Quince Puree

  • 8 whole quinces
  • 1 litre pear juice
  • 200ml lemon juice
  • 300g caster sugar
  • 1 litre water

Pickled Pear

  • 4x wax tip Williams pears
  • 200g ginger
  • 500ml litre water
  • 250g caster sugar
  • 250g Chardonnay vinegar

Puy Lentils

  • 400g puy lentils
  • 1x carrot
  • 2x shallots
  • 2 cloves of garlic
  • 1 stick celery
  • Sprig of thyme
  • 100ml white wine

Method

  • Start by making the quince purée. Bring to the boil lemon juice, pear juice, water and sugar. Peel, quarter, deseed and slice the quinces then place into the poaching liquid. Simmer until tender, strain and blitz. Add some of the poaching liquid back to the purée until the correct consistency is reached then pass through a sieve and chill.
  • Now make the pickled pear. Peel and finely julienne the ginger before blanching. Now make a syrup with the water, sugar and vinegar then add the blanched ginger. Peel, quarter and deseed the pears and finely slice. Steep the sliced pears into the hot ginger syrup and set aside.
  • Now turn to the puy lentils. Finely chop the shallot, carrot, garlic, thyme and celery and sweat in a heavy bottomed pan and cook until caramelised. Deglaze with white wine and cook out. Add the washed lentils to the pan and cover in water, bring to a simmer and cook for approximately 15 minutes making sure the lentils still have a bite. Leave the lentils to cool in the liquid.
  • To prepare the partridges, remove the wishbone with a small sharp knife. Then, using a sharp pair of scissors, cut along both sides of the spine and remove it. Lay the birds on a board with the breasts facing up, and press down on the middle of the breast to flatten them slightly. Season both sides of the birds well with sea salt.
  • Set the same pan over medium heat with a splash of oil, and lay the partridges in, skin side down. Once the pan is sizzling, reduce the heat to low and place a weight on top of the birds. Cook for 6-8 minutes, then flip the birds and turn off the heat.
  • Dice the chorizo and saute in butter, once coloured add the lentils along with some of the lentil cooking liquid. Adjust seasoning and finish with chopped parsley before serving up.

FTSE 100 wealth manager St James’s Place (SJP) has been hit with High Court legal action by one of its largest former partner firms, Wellesley Investment Management.

West Sussex-based Wellesley was previously one of SJP’s largest advice firms, operating as a self-employed practice within its partnership network.

The wealth advisory firm managed £1bn in funds and was once recognised as one of SJP’s largest practices by funds under management.

In July, Wellesley ended its relationship with SJP to join the UK network of the Swedish wealth management group Söderberg & Partners.

In its announcement, the firm said: “By joining the Söderberg & Partners network, we combine the personal relationships and tailored advice that define Wellesley, with the investment expertise, scale and innovation of an international organisation overseeing more than £100bn in assets under advice.”

At the time, reports said the advisory firm left the FTSE giant’s network around the same time as another SJP firm, Sheffield-based Prospera Wealth Management. The firm has since joined Söderberg & Partners Financial Planning.

Court action

On Wednesday, the High Court showed that Wellesley had instructed specialist disputes law firm Signature Litigation to file a case against St James’s Place Wealth Management plc, St James’s Place Management Services and St James’s Place Partnership Services.

SJP declined to comment. Wellesley was contacted for comment. It is understood that the case was filed with the Commercial Court, but the formal statement of case has yet to be served to the defendants.

In July, it was reported that SJP took a £1bn hit to net inflows in the first half of the year as investors pulled cash from its funds to dodge market volatility and a looming pension tax bill. Its net inflows declined from £3.8bn to £2.7bn in the first half of the year, in line with analyst expectations. The group pinned the decline on market uncertainty coupled with “impending changes” to the retirement and financial planning landscape.

]]> 2484108Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan Dan Evans risks backlash by playing in Gazprom-funded Russia tennis event https://www.cityam.com/dan-evans-risks-backlash-by-playing-in-gazprom-funded-russia-tennis-event/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:51:23 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2484122

Davis Cup hero and former British No1 Dan Evans has risked criticism by coming out of retirement to play in a tennis tournament hosted in and funded by Russia. Evans is among eight non-Russians in the 12-person field for the Northern Palmyra Trophies mixed doubles exhibition tournament taking place in St Petersburg from today until [...]]]>

Davis Cup hero and former British No1 Dan Evans has risked criticism by coming out of retirement to play in a tennis tournament hosted in and funded by Russia.

Evans is among eight non-Russians in the 12-person field for the Northern Palmyra Trophies mixed doubles exhibition tournament taking place in St Petersburg from today until Sunday.

The event is being financed by Gazprom, the state-owned energy giant whose sponsorship of football’s Champions League was terminated by Uefa when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Russia remains a pariah in the sporting world as a result of its attacks on Ukraine, with its national teams and clubs banned in football, rugby union, basketball and athletics.

Evans, 36, retired from professional tennis after this year’s Wimbledon but agreed to dust off his racket for the Northern Palmyra Trophies. It is not known what fee he is receiving.

Other players taking part include Frenchmen Adrian Mannarino, 38, and Corentin Moutet, who was fined £30,000 for swearing seven times in a live BBC interview at Queen’s Club last year.

Former world top 10 players Janko Tipsarevic, of Serbia, and Alexander Bublik, who was born in Russia but represents Kazakhstan, and Russian Karen Khachanov are also on the bill.

Completing the line-up are Kamilla Rakhimova of Uzbekistan, Anastasia Potapova, who was born in Russia but now represents Austria, Elena Vesnina, Yulia Putintseva, Diana Shnaider and Anna Pushkareva.

Dan Evans’ career mixed controversy with glory

Evans has previously overcome controversy to become a popular figure in British tennis and part of the Great Britain team that won the Davis Cup in 2015.

His national funding was suspended aged 18 after he was pictured in a nightclub hours before a match at Wimbledon and cut altogether two years later for poor performance.

After re-establishing himself and helping Andy Murray lead Britain to Davis Cup glory he received a one-year ban from tennis in 2017 after testing positive for cocaine.

He rebuilt his career again, becoming British No1 in 2019, winning his first ATP Tour title in 2021 and reaching a career-high 21 in the world rankings in 2023.

In 2024 he played alongside Murray as the latter bowed out of professional tennis at the Paris Olympics and this summer hung up his own racket.

Russia has been creeping back into top-level sport, with the International Olympic Committee’s reinstatement in June paving the way for a team at the LA28 Games.

The country won a legal battle to be allowed back into international ice hockey just weeks ago, although the decision has been met with resistance by much of the sport.

]]> 2484122Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres Chinese e-commerce giants could starve high streets of Black Friday boost https://www.cityam.com/chinese-e-commerce-giants-could-starve-high-streets-of-black-friday-boost/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:43:23 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2484040

Chinese retail giants like Temu and Shein could be the big winners from this year’s Black Friday, as high street shops are starved of “make or break” footfall, industry figures have warned. Overseas e-commerce firms are able to avoid paying tax on any imports worth less than £135 as part of a tax loophole known [...]]]>

Chinese retail giants like Temu and Shein could be the big winners from this year’s Black Friday, as high street shops are starved of “make or break” footfall, industry figures have warned.

Overseas e-commerce firms are able to avoid paying tax on any imports worth less than £135 as part of a tax loophole known as the ‘de-minimis’ threshold. Retailers have long campaigned for this rule to be scrapped, warning they face an uneven playing field. 

The British Independent Retailers Association, a trade body representing the high street, said it is “concerned” many UK shops will miss out on crucial Black Friday trading because Brits are opting to stay at home and order goods cheaper online.

Jeff Moody, the group’s chief operating officer, told City AM: “Overseas platforms start every sale with an advantage British retailers can’t match. Independent retailers can’t afford to slash margins the way the ultra-low-cost Chinese platforms do, and most don’t try. 

“They compete on expertise, service and being part of their community. But when the rules are tilted against them, good businesses lose sales they should be winning.”

He added that the so-called golden quarter – which includes Black Friday and the Christmas shopping period – “makes or breaks the year for many independents”.

Black Friday has always been a crucial period for retailers since the US tradition spread to the UK, but recent hikes to business rates and employment costs mean high street businesses need this extra revenue more than ever.

Moody added: “The money they take between now and Christmas carries them through the quiet months of January and February. If that trade doesn’t come, some will struggle to survive into the spring.”

The government has committed to closing the de-minimis loophole but this rule change will not come into force until October 2028 – having been accelerated from an initial deadline of March 2029. 

Long wait for tax crackdown

Dan Tomlinson, exchequer secretary to the Treasury, said when announcing the crackdown that the government would “tackle the unfair competition and dodgy businesses that are doing real damage to our high streets”.

But retailers have urged the government to move quicker, warning that recent clampdowns in the US and the EU mean that e-commerce firms are increasingly targeting UK shoppers because they now face higher taxes in these other markets. 

The value of Chinese parcel imports below the £135 threshold soared from £1.3bn to £5.3bn in the two fiscal years to 2025-26, according to recent HMRC data obtained by the Financial Times.

Tom Ironside, director of policy at the British Retail Consortium, said: “UK retailers have called for the same approach as the EU: tariffs on goods, alongside an administrative fee to cover the cost of customs. 

“The key difference is that the EU has put these measures in place already, while UK retailers will have to wait until October 2028 for action. That means two more years of inaction, increasing the risk that the UK becomes even more attractive to overseas online sellers.”

At the Budget last month, John Healey said online retailers will be made responsible for collecting VAT from the sellers which use their platforms, in a bid to equalise the tax burden between these firms and the high street.

These new rules will apply to all sellers whose annual revenue exceeds £90,000 but some tax experts have said this threshold should be dropped to zero. “Unless that happens these Chinese sham companies will find just another way around the rules,” said Tax Policy Associates founder Dan Neidle.

Modern sport is obsessed with the future: innovation, disruption, new formats, new audiences. Yet paradoxically the things that often make sport matter are old-fashioned: records, rivalries, heroes and history.

It’s why starting a new sporting competition is such a difficult business. You can build it but – to paraphrase Field of Dreams – will they come? The last few weeks have shown the knife-edge of that gamble.

We’ve seen rugby’s inaugural Nations Championship and Uefa’s Nations League burst into life, while on the other side of the coin (and it’s a mighty big coin) LIV Golf has found a bunker it can’t escape from.

It got me thinking: it can’t just be luck, or funding. There must be some science to why some competitions succeed and others stutter. And increasingly that answer lies not in economics but in sociology. 

Before we start comparing apples with oranges, I should note that, of course, not all new competitions are the same.

You have creationary competitions that build something entirely new, often giving growing sports a competitive stage for the first time. Examples include the UFC, X Games and Premier Padel Tour. 

Then you have evolutionary competitions that take something familiar and give it a new environment. The Nations League and Nations Championship both fall into this category, so too the Laver Cup in tennis and football’s Club World Cup.  

Finally, you have revolutionary competitions. The IPL, Formula E, The Hundred, TGL, King’s League, LIV;  they are noisiest and most controversial but face the highest risk of failing. 

Despite these differences, they’re all trying to change fan behaviour. And their chance of success is not defined by money but meaning. 

Jeopardy, belonging, proof and lore

Meaning is everything in sport and it is an infuriatingly fragile thing for marketers to deal with. Hard to build and easy to break but, without it, new competitions don’t stand a chance.

The first challenge is jeopardy. For sport to mean anything, something needs to be on the line. Not just what you stand to win, but what you stand to lose. A trophy, a title, a place in the next round. 

LIV Golf’s organisers thought they were doing the right thing by creating the sport’s biggest financial prizes, but they failed to understand what any gambler will tell you: it’s also what you stand to lose that makes it matter. 

The second rule is belonging. People don’t just want to watch sport; they want to be part of it. This is what the IPL understood so brilliantly, giving cities their own teams and creating new loyalties. Similarly, the X Games gave a generation of action-sports fans a competition that reflected them and their culture. 

Belonging means a supporter is tying their fate to the supported. When they win the fan wins and vice versa. You can’t just invent that. It comes from a deeper social need, that a sporting team or individual becomes an extension of a fan’s own identity. 

The third principle is proof. Sport has meaning when that meaning is shared. Like money, it only has value if other people believe in it too. 

Sold-out stadiums and big broadcast deals help – one of the biggest coups for the Nations Championship was securing wall-to-wall coverage on ITV – but visibility is not the same as proof. 

Proof comes from how deeply people care. This is perhaps what King’s League and other influencer-led competitions struggle to understand. 

The final way to create meaning is through lore. By now we’re all familiar with the Drive To Survive effect, but while stories are powerful, legends are more so. 

Lore is not just about storytelling; it’s about history. Wales’s victory over New Zealand in the Nations Championship mattered because it was their first in a lifetime. 

This doesn’t mean new competitions can’t bring a freshness to sport, but if they can borrow from or tap into sporting lore then they are that much more likely to create the meaning that they need.

Most important facets are too often an afterthought

There they are; four rules to create meaning. Simple in theory, but perhaps less so in practice. And yet I suspect they’re often an afterthought when people set out to create a new sporting competition. 

The first conversation will usually be financial. How much do we need? Who’s going to invest? But if I was about to start a new competition, I would be focusing my energy more on meaning that money. 

Matt Readman is chief strategy officer at sports creative agency Dark Horses.

    There was a lot of coverage globally when Space X floated in June this year. Over 100,000 UK investors applied for shares (almost $1bn of orders) in what was the largest IPO in history. At the same time – others across the globe, including Germany, France, Japan, Australia and Canada were also investing. None of these countries had to re-write its rules to enable this as each of them used a gateway which was already established and set up. In the UK, this was the ‘Public Offer Platform Regime’ which the FCA brought into play this January. This effectively lets companies raising over £5m sell shares widely without a stock market listing.

    SpaceX was offering retail investors the opportunity to invest on the same terms as the big banks and institutions “pre-IPO”.  In many respects, the risk of the business mirror those of many private companies looking to scale up in the UK, just on a global scale. The time has come for a grown-up discussion about the benefits of investing in these types of companies as part of a diversified portfolio.

    Most of the growth of a company now happens before most of us get the opportunity to ‘buy in’. By the time everyday investors get their chance, much of the value has already gone to the funds and wealthy investors who were able to get in early. I think that if we want people to be able to share in the growth of the companies that they use every day then access before they list on the public markets matters as much as gaining access after an IPO.

    Of course, regulated crowdfunding (the UK being one of its pioneers) has been working to achieve this for more than a decade now yet the gateways that worked for Space X don’t work for (for example) a small fast-growing company in Manchester seeking investors from outside the UK.     What seems to be holding things back is a lack understanding and mutual recognition. Firms have strict limits on how much they can raise, compliance costs for platforms are huge, disclosures can’t easily be compared between countries and settlements are slow (and manual) for smaller issuers. But importantly each jurisdiction writes its rules in isolation treating the world outside the national boundary as almost irrelevant.

    Research from the Global Equity Crowdfunding Alliance (GECA) suggests that the fixes to these should be achievable by the policymakers, regulators and platforms that are in place now. I guess at the minute what is missing is the ambition to have it all joined up across borders. But that’s where GECA steps in.

These core principles underpin the vast majority of the big financial decisions adults will make in their lives, from taking out a mortgage, deciding which credit card offers the best value or investing in an ISA. The report shows how much further as a society we need to go to put numeracy on an equal footing with literacy. Can you imagine the reaction if it was revealed 8m adults had the literacy skills of a nine-year-old? It would rightly generate immediate action; yet the fact the same number share the numeracy skills of a year four pupil does not. 

    Numeracy and the workforce

    Over recent months, my Committee heard from employers ranging from Santander and Barclays to National Grid, EDF and BT. Many said numeracy was a problem that needed attention, and many are running their own catch-up training programmes to get their employees up to speed. 

    But the industries of tomorrow will make us even more reliant on having a workforce that’s confident in its numbers. Employers told us that artificial intelligence in particular is increasing the need for better numeracy. 

    Central to this is a shift from calculation to judgement. That is, knowing whether the answer a chatbot produces actually makes sense. From financial services to energy and the digital economy, the sectors that will power Britain’s growth will depend on the workforce of tomorrow having the right judgement.

    So ministers should treat this announcement as a first step. Two more would make a real difference.

    What else is needed

    First, the teachers delivering these lessons are often not maths specialists. They need proper training in the concepts themselves, not just a new set of lesson plans. We all know the positive impact an engaging teacher can have. 

    Second, the red tape that makes it harder for employers to get into classrooms should be cut. The businesses we heard from are eager to show pupils why numbers matter, and we should let them. Too often pupils can’t see how the maths they learn in the classroom connects to the world of work. Seeing it applied would be transformational.

    The government is clearly listening and I commend them for it. However, if we are to tackle the systemic societal issues caused by poor numeracy it must now go further. I will be the first to praise them if they do.

    The race to be the next Mayor of London has started and it’s the Conservatives who have been first out of the blocks

    Being Mayor of London is like being Spiderman: with great power comes great responsibility – but also opportunity. Whoever wins truly has the chance to shape one of the greatest cities in the world. 

    Not just theoretically or politically but physically. The Mayor has powers to reshape the city, from transport infrastructure and building homes to ensuring the multiple villages that make up London thrive. As an architect, I always feel that London does best when its Mayors take a passion and interest in architecture and the built environment. 

    London’s architecture is the jewel in its crown. I moved to London in the Blair era, eager to study architecture at the Bartlett. I arrived just weeks after the 7/7 bombings, and London’s resilience made me proud. “We are Londoners” was everywhere, a shared determination to keep going. Alongside it was a tangible ambition to build. London had won the Olympic bid and it felt like anything was possible. London’s skyline was transformed. There was ambition about what London could become. Ken Livingstone appointed Richard Rogers as his chief adviser on architecture and urbanism, and the architecture and urbanism unit brought design into the heart of City Hall. Architecture wasn’t simply something that happened as a consequence of development. It was part of a wider vision for the capital.

    Boris Johnson also took an interest. Like or loathe the Garden Bridge, the proposed Thames Estuary airport or the ArcelorMittal Orbit, they were big ideas. They showed an appetite for thinking about London at a city-wide scale.

    Look north too. As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham put place at the centre of his politics. He used Mayoral Development Corporations to drive regeneration from Stockport to Old Trafford.

    Sadiq Khan’s approach has been quieter on architecture, although his mayoralty has faced huge challenges. On air quality, particularly through the expansion of ULEZ, he has demonstrated the scale of change that mayors can pursue.

A decision driven by the desire to save rather than a vision of what London’s civic heart should look like. And in any case, as Lord John of Southwark, former council leader, argued on my Architects for Change podcast, even those savings warrant scrutiny.

    Somewhere along the way, we seem to have lost the confidence to think big about our city. Now, London needs that confidence back.

    Urban renaissance

    We need an urban renaissance and we need to build. London’s built environment is worth £111bn a year, 19 per cent of the city’s economy, and supports more than 620,000 jobs. But the construction sector currently feels worse than 2008. London’s housebuilding is collapsing and the money is leaving.

    London’s success has always depended on its ability to attract talent, investment and ideas. But increasingly, the very people who make London such a creative, vibrant and exciting place cannot afford to live here. That includes the young architects, designers and builders who will actually shape the city.

    London is currently home to some of the world’s most celebrated architecture practices, alongside hundreds of smaller studios. London’s chartered practices alone turn over £2.8bn a year. They create the buildings, streets and neighbourhoods that act as attractive adverts for a London people want to visit, work and live in.

    How do we make London greener, healthier, more affordable and more beautiful?

    The answer lies not just in architecture and creative urbanism but political leadership.

    The next Mayor, whoever it is, whatever their rosette needs to champion the built environment, not simply as an economic driver, but as one of the most powerful tools we have to tackle inequality, respond to climate change and improve people’s lives.

    And frankly I want some fabulousness too. Some sparkle. Buildings and public spaces that inspire us and that Londoners can feel proud of. Why not appoint a City Architect to drive that collective longer term ambition? 

    Of course, London’s finances are challenging. The housing delivery model is under severe strain, and the next Mayor will inherit difficult decisions. But that makes ambition more important, not less. We need action to get London building again, not just for today’s Londoners who desperately need homes, but for Londoners of the future too.

    I want to see the next Mayor be passionate about the built environment and give London its mojo back. I’m calling for nothing short of an urban renaissance.

    A relentless wave of regulatory reform in the pensions sector is “overwhelming” providers and placing them under operational strain, a senior Schroders executive has said.

    Rachel Harris, head of UK Institutional at the FTSE 100 funds group, said the stream of consultations, legislative changes and regulatory frameworks brought forward by government and regulators has triggered a “seismic change” across Britain’s retirement savings industry.

    Pension providers, typically workplace schemes and master trusts, have seen an overhaul ranging from the Pension Schemes Act, the incoming Value for Money framework, and a fresh consultation from the Financial Conduct Authority into the pension charge cap.

    In an interview with City AM, Harris said: “Some of this stuff needs to be done. But I do think it has led to pretty seismic changes in terms of how we think about pensions in the UK.

    “Every week there’s another piece of news out there on pension schemes you don’t necessarily expect.”

    She noted that while asset managers like Schroders are able to manage the wave of change through public policy teams, for the actual providers it can be hard to manage the workload, particularly as both the government and City watchdog are introducing various policies and consultations.

    “Trying to keep up with all the different policy frameworks that are being issued by all the various different regulators…not necessarily so much for us sitting in asset management, but if you think about the actual providers and how overwhelming it is for them, I think it can be really difficult,” she said.

    Large managers and master trusts boast sizable internal policy teams to manage the workload coming off the back of policy shakeups, but smaller single-employer trusts face a more difficult challenge in managing changes, Harris warned.

    In particular, the Value for Money framework, which is set to be implemented from 2028, has faced backlash for placing a greater burden on smaller schemes. 

    Master trusts spread fixed governance and reporting costs across thousands of members, but smaller schemes must compile the same annual datasets across a much smaller base, driving up costs and pushing more towards consolidation.

    Plans for guided retirement

    Pensions minister Torsten Bell also recently unveiled plans for an overhaul of how private workers could draw their pensions in a bid to close the retirement gap between the public and private sector.

    Joint proposals from the Department for Work and Pensions, the FCA and the Pensions Regulator outlined that providers will be required to offer workers an annual income as standard in retirement. 

    The plans, dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, will “resurrect” the option of having an inflation protected pension that provides a secure income for private sector retirees and prevents them from having to make complex financial decisions. 

    Harris, who was appointed head of UK Institutional in March of this year, noted that private sector providers “haven’t had to do [this] up until now”, but the growing number of defined contribution savers and retirees has forced the issue onto the government agenda.

    She also added the UK is ahead of Australia when it comes to helping savers turn their pots into steady retirement income, despite the country often being held as the gold standard for workplace pensions.

    “They’ve had super funds going forever… we’re actually ahead of them on retirement income thinking, which I find slightly peculiar,” she said.

    While critics have warned that pooling savers into collective schemes risks stripping away personal choice and flexibility, Harris stressed that proposals, known as collective defined contribution (CDC) schemes, are designed as an optional safety net rather than a one-size-fits-all mandate.

    “CDC is an option. It’s not the only option. For some people it will work and it will make things better, which is the whole point of us trying to fix the retirement problem,” she said.

    She added that appetite for collective schemes is primarily concentrated among “paternalistic” employers and family-run businesses “where it is…a more palatable option”.

    The heavy regulatory backdrop comes as policymakers lean on DC schemes to channel billions into the UK economy through the Mansion House Accord.

    Under the agreement, 17 of the top providers, including Aviva and Aegon UK, agreed to allocate at least 10 per cent of default assets to private markets by 2030. Five per cent of this total is earmarked for the UK.

    But the agreement has come under scrutiny. Despite 3.3 per cent of assets being allocated to private markets, according to the latest update from the Association of British Insurers, the allocation is heavily skewed away from equities.

    “You can set up a pension fund, but you’re going to have a board of trustees, and the trustees have a fiduciary duty,” Harris said. “The fiduciary duty… is to provide them with the best possible risk-adjusted returns.”

    While acknowledging frustrations from venture capital managers that pension funds are moving “too slow”, Harris noted that trustees must balance domestic ambitions against diversification.

    Altria Group, whose companies also include Philip Morris USA, told markets on Thursday it is in early talks regarding a takeover of Imperial Brands but no agreement has yet been reached.

    Under UK takeover rules, Altria will has until 5pm on December 24 to announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away. The London market will close at lunchtime on Christmas Eve.

    Imperial Brand shares were up 16 per cent on the news to 3,472p. The firm, whose brands include Golden Virginia and JPS, commands a £26bn market valuation.

    Bloomberg previously reported that Japan Tobacco was evaluating a potential acquisition ⁠of Imperial Brands.

    Threat of FTSE 100 exodus continues

    The group’s departure from the City would ramp up pressure on the stock market after foreign buyers and private equity buyers swooped on London-listed companies throughout 2026.

    US property giant Prologis tabled a £14bn takeover for FTSE 100 real estate firm Segro earlier this year, while Easyjet was taken private by Apollo for £5.7bn.

    The takeover talks follow Imperial Brands confirming it will cut between 2,100 and 2,500 further jobs across its international operations before 2030. This follows the firm already reducing its headcount by 2,100 in the last financial year.

    “Throughout this transformation, we are committed to following appropriate consultation processes and supporting our people,” the firm told shareholders. 

    The Bristol-based firm saw its revenue fall by 1.5 per cent to £31.7bn in the year to September. Its operating profit dipped by 10 per cent to £3.1bn, which the group blamed in part on its cost-savings programme.

    Lukas Paravicini, chief executive officer of the firm, said: “While continuing to invest in and build future consumer capabilities, underpinned by new technologies, we are confident of achieving at least £320 million of annual savings by 2030.”

    Making their way to work on Thursday morning, Poundland’s thousands of staff couldn’t help but wonder how many more commutes they had left. In the discount retailer’s near-600 stores across the country, shop workers were briefed via conference call by Barry Williams, Poundland’s managing director, and Alix Partners, who will oversee the company’s administration. 

    Williams told staff “today should have been a day of celebration given the unique turnaround of the business on the high street,” one Poundland employee said. In conversations at the retailer’s stores and in its Walsall headquarters, staff have expressed their “thanks” to its management and “concern” over the decisions made by Gordon Brothers, its owner, another said.

    “While [it was] difficult news to share, there was support from colleagues for Barry’s efforts over recent weeks and it finished with a round of applause for him. He’s much loved by the colleagues,” another person with knowledge of the briefing said.

    ‘We turned Poundland around’

    Poundland’s management and its owners have been split over whether the retailer is showing signs of improvement. Williams told staff on Wednesday they had worked “tirelessly” to return the company to growth, amid reports that Poundland is on track for an £18m profit.

    But Gordon Brothers have insisted that the retailer remains “vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin” and had not completed its recovery.

    Poundland’s staff are overwhelmingly supportive of Williams and have been disappointed by the investment firm’s messaging, one employee said. “We’ve all worked our absolute damnedest to turn the business round, and we’ve done it.”

    A virtual ‘thank-you’ card addressed to Barry Williams is circulating among Poundland’s workers and the volume of messages has stretched the document to more than 160 pages, sources said.

    Another employee said they don’t know when stores will begin to close, though the company considers its staff to be “at risk.” They added: “It’s certainly been a difficult and uncertain period for employees, particularly with the concerns about job security and the future of the business.”

    Meanwhile, Poundland’s administrators are being flooded with emails. Alix Partners has already received dozens of ‘kite-flying’ inquiries into the retailer, feigning interest at buying either the whole company or some of its stores, sources said.

    The administrators’ first task will be to wade through their packed inboxes and determine which of these approaches are genuine, and which are opportunistic. Top of Alix Partners’ list will be Xyra Group Holdings, Martin Property Group, Premier Quality Foods and Zachert Private Equity, who had all been vying to buy the retailer solvently in the hours before its collapse.

    Gordon Brothers decided none of these bids could be completed before a court order stalling Poundland’s creditors was due to lapse. Though each of these bidders had been hoping to buy the retailer as a going concern, Xyra and Premier have already expressed their interest in buying the company out of consideration.

    These proposals will be prioritised by administrators, sources said, because they have already completed much of the work towards a deal, including due diligence and lining up their funding. 

    Administrators face huge task

    In a statement provided to Sky News, Premier owner Idris Mohammed claimed he had not been able to stump up “enough funding to address the historic liabilities while still leaving sufficient cash in the business to pay staff and suppliers, replenish stock and keep the shelves full”.

    One industry observer described this as an “extraordinary” admission. The government has faced calls to partially fund a takeover of Poundland’s in order to protect jobs. Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, has urged ministers to “help bridge finance” for a sale, though people close to the process have said this would be unlikely.

    Beyond the immediate future facing Poundland and its 11,000 workers, the retailer’s collapse will send shockwaves through the UK’s high streets. The administration makes it more likely that the company will be broken up between a host of retail buyers.

    Poundland’s stores will continue trading for now and no job losses will occur immediately, people close to the matter said, though administrators have not yet worked out how much longer the business can continue to run.

    An industry source said they expect Alix Partners to go “back out to the market” and review existing and new bids for the retailer “from scratch”. The process to find a buyer was being run by City advisory firm Alvarez & Marsal before Poundland’s administration but this responsibility switched to Alix Partners as soon as the retailer collapsed. 

    Staff at the New-York based consultancy will now be racing to get to grips with the reams of performance data, takeover proposals and funding documents involved in the attempted sale, though they had been drawing up contingency plans for a number of weeks.

    A spokesperson for the administrators said on Wednesday that they welcome approaches from “anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities”.

    Many of the retailers interested in buying just parts of Poundland have already committed to taking on all the employees at the stores they would acquire, though staff at sites which are not bought could lose their jobs. 

    High street shake-up

    If Poundland is split apart by administrators, this process would see high street stalwarts like Tesco, Lidl, Iceland, B&M and The Range tussle to pick up the best-quality space in the UK’s towns and cities. The retailers which get their choice of stores will be given a significant leg-up in the intense battle to woo Britain’s increasingly cash-strapped shoppers.

    Since its foundation in 1991, Poundland has become a staple of high streets across the UK, building up to a footprint of about 600 stores. Should the retailer’s brand cease to exist as part of this administration, discount rivals like B&M and Home Bargains will hope to gain more shoppers looking for cheap groceries and discounted homeware.

    But Poundland’s struggles will give pause to its competitors. In theory, the retailer’s huge footprint and cheap products would have positioned it well to capitalise on the cost-of-living crisis, though it ultimately failed to stay afloat.

    Poundland’s collapse has already provoked questions over the role of private equity in the UK’s high streets. Gordon Brothers has been bruised by its attempted sale of the retailer, during which time it has been dubbed an asset-stripper and a “high street raider”.

    Parliament’s business select committee, which subjected the US investment firm to a two-hour grilling earlier this month, has demanded that it stays away from Poundland in future, by not taking up the potentially lucrative role of liquidating its stock. 

    Andy Street, a former Tory regional mayor and boss of John Lewis, has urged the government to use insolvency rules to “go after” Gordon Brothers “with the full force of the law”. He said earlier this month: “I do not yet believe the government has gone as far as it should in protecting these jobs.”

    Each week, we dig into the memory bank of the City’s great and good. Today, Paul Sherwin, managing director at workplace design firm Oktra, takes us through his career

    CV

    • Name: Paul Sherwin
    • Job title: Managing director at Oktra
    • Previous roles: MD at Maris Interiors; senior designer at Morgan Lovell
    • Age: 51
    • Born: Surrey, England
    • Lives: Bromley, Kent
    • Studied: BA (Hons) Design at Leeds Metropolitan University
    • Talents: Spotting potential in people and helping them grow into it. I love mentoring and pushing people to develop professionally.
    • Motto: Maximum joy, minimum fuss!
    • Biggest perk of the job: Turning a client’s ideas for their office into reality, then seeing those spaces come to life across the City and the London skyline.
    • Coffee order: Latte with whole milk
    • Cocktail order: Negroni
    • Favourite book: 1984 by George Orwell
    • Comfort movie: The Shawshank Redemption

    What was your first job?

    Working at my dad’s local rugby club at age 10. I’m not sure that would be legal nowadays! It was great training in customer service and mental maths. The pay wasn’t too bad either: a bottle of Coke and a Mars bar for an afternoon’s work.

    What was your first role in the big city?

    I started out in London as a designer at a large design and construction business, a couple of years after graduating in Design from Leeds Metropolitan University. It was a very junior role, but I was hungry for growth and professional development, and I’m grateful for where it took me.

    When did you know you wanted to build a career in the City?

    I have always loved London. It’s where the best companies and talent connect to the global market, and as someone who consults with big companies, there’s no better place to work. This is where the best work, buildings and projects are happening.

    What’s one thing you love about the City of London?

    I love the variety. So many areas of London have their own distinct identity – from the corporate grit of the City, to the classic elegance of Mayfair and the hustle and bustle of Soho.

    And one thing you would change?

    Fewer traffic jams.

    What’s been your most memorable business lunch?

    Meetings in the private dining room at Berry Bros. & Rudd are always memorable. It’s Britain’s oldest wine and spirit merchant, and the building itself is steeped in history, with the original timber floors and underground vaults. The chefs prepare a delicious lunch while an expert sommelier talks you through the wine pairings. Clients love it, and it’s helped us secure more than one new partnership.

    And any business faux pas?

    A wet handshake! Lesson learned: dry your hands properly after washing them, before any client handshake. First impressions are everything, and no one likes a damp hand.

    What’s been your proudest moment?

    Consulting with world-class companies like Deliveroo, Adidas and Lindt to shape their property decisions. It all helps to build happier teams, stronger performance and profitability, and above all, provide great spaces for people to work.

    And who do you look up to?

    My partner is the headteacher at a London comprehensive, and she’s responsible for 900 kids and 150 staff. So when I think I’ve had a bad day, I look at her and she brings me back to earth. Watching her give every child a shot at a brighter future is incredibly humbling.

    What’s the best career advice you’ve ever been given?

    Success is more about attitude than academic excellence. Some people are born into opportunity, but most of us have to earn it through graft and results. It tastes a lot sweeter when you’ve had to earn it.

    And the worst?

    That you’ve gone as far as you can go in your career. Be brave – if you know in your heart that you’ve got more to offer, ask for it, and if it doesn’t come, move on. Don’t waste precious time waiting for someone to give you a chance.

    Are you optimistic for the year ahead?

    It’s exciting and daunting in equal measure. AI is developing so rapidly, and it will radically reshape every business we work with and how we operate – including why people
    come into the office and what that space needs to offer them in the long term. This is both an opportunity and a challenge.

    We’re going for lunch, and you’re picking. Where are we going?

    Farmer J, every time, for a salad or a high-protein hot lunch. The concept of quality food served fast has really taken off in London, and they do it better than most. If you’re hungry, Blacklock for a steak or Brigadiers for a curry are my top recommendations.

    And if we’re grabbing a drink after work?

    Somewhere you can actually talk, particularly with a small group. City Arts Bar on Ironmonger Lane is a dark, cosy room with velvet armchairs and quiet corners, and it’s the kind of place where the more sensitive conversations happen.

    Where’s home during the week?

    Bromley. I’m there most weekends too, but I’ll head into London for a culture fix at the iconic galleries or the ballet. Other times, it’s just to enjoy a great English pub and a pint of Guinness.

    And where might we find you at the weekend?

    I’m a huge live music fan, so you’ll find me at gigs at Brixton Academy or the Hammersmith Apollo. On a quieter night, I love to stroll round Soho and enjoy counter dining at Pulpo or Kiln.

    You’ve got a well-deserved two weeks off. Where are you going and who with?

    Somewhere hot with my partner and our kids. When the kids were younger, it was all about places that kept them busy in the day, and now they’re older, we’re looking further afield. Texas, Tokyo and Abu Dhabi are all on our bucket list.

    Changes to the law mean companies – including football clubs – can now be held liable for offences such as child abuse by their senior management and owners, write lawyers Helen Harvey and Charlotte Moss.     Changes to the law mean companies – including football clubs – can now be held liable for offences such as child abuse by their senior management and owners, write lawyers Helen Harvey and Charlotte Moss.

    Earlier this month, the Football Association launched Voices of Truth, a digital platform paying tribute to survivors of child sexual abuse in football.

    It marked 10 years since revelations by former footballers led the FA to commission an independent inquiry into historic abuse, which culminated in the Sheldon Review in 2021. But the anniversary is not just a moment to remember; it brings renewed attention on where accountability for misconduct in football should lie today.

    A recent change in the law raises an important question: could clubs themselves be prosecuted for alleged abuse by individuals? Since June, under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, companies can be held criminally liable for offences committed by senior managers while acting in the course of their role.  

    A senior manager is someone who plays a significant role in making decisions about, or managing, the whole or a substantial part of a company’s activities. But determining who counts as a senior manager is not straightforward.

    Prosecutors will look beyond an individual’s job title, employment status or pay to consider their influence over how the business is run. Government guidance makes clear that directors and senior officers, such as CFOs and COOs, would normally fall within the definition. Club owners may too, depending on how involved they are in its running. 

    However, senior management is not limited to board members or those performing executive roles, and could include those with significant responsibility for functions such as HR.

    For football clubs, this could extend to individuals not traditionally considered senior management. For example, coaches or those responsible for player selection, managing player contracts or overseeing a club’s grassroots programme could be caught, depending on their responsibilities. 

    Clubs may need to review safeguarding measures

    Crucially, the offence must have been committed while the senior manager was acting within the “actual or apparent scope of their authority”. This does not mean that the criminal conduct was authorised in some way – it just means it happened when the person was doing their job. 

    For instance, a coach who sexually assaults a player while demonstrating a technique during a training drill may be considered to be acting within the scope of their authority as the conduct occurred in the course of their coaching duties. The same could apply to a club CEO who uses a meeting about a player’s contract or future at the club to commit a sexual offence. 

    However, with no case law to consider, it is not yet clear who will qualify as a senior manager and when their conduct will fall within the scope of their authority. 

    The Act also makes it a criminal offence to deliberately prevent or discourage someone from reporting suspected child sexual abuse where they are legally required to do so. Although this “obstruction offence” has not yet come into force, once implemented, it could give rise to corporate liability if committed by a senior manager acting within the scope of their authority.

    Where allegations of criminal misconduct arise, football clubs must now consider their own potential corporate exposure, rather than dealing with the matter solely through internal disciplinary proceedings and individual accountability.

    Clubs may therefore want to revisit their training and safeguarding procedures to ensure they are robust and that the responsibilities of those in senior positions, including coaching staff, are clearly understood. 

    A decade on from survivors’ bravery in disclosing their experiences, the onus is now well and truly on clubs to do everything in their power to stamp out abuse.

    Helen Harvey is a Senior Associate and Charlotte Moss an Associate in the Corporate Crime and Investigations team at Michelman & Robinson UK LLP.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.
