]]>
Latvian carrier airBaltic is reportedly offering some of its pilots the opportunity to work for Papua New Guinea’s national airline as the struggling carrier seeks to reduce costs during its Chapter 11 restructuring.

The proposals, reported by Reuters, include temporary secondments to Air Niugini, where pilots would fly the airline’s Airbus A220s from next year.

airBaltic seeks to cuts costs amid Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings

The other options apparently offered to the airBaltic pilots include taking a demotion – such as senior pilots relinquishing line training captain positions, which attract additional pay – reduced flying and voluntary redundancy.

The measures form part of an effort to reduce staffing costs as airBaltic scales back its operation amid mounting financial pressure. 

Details of the proposals were contained in internal correspondence seen by Reuters and confirmed by two people familiar with the process.

Last month, it was revealed that airBaltic was preparing to cut between 500 and 700 jobs.

The proposed reductions were said to affect employees across the airline’s bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn, with the carrier consulting with unions over changes to working arrangements.

airBaltic said the redundancies would ensure the “company’s structure and cost base are aligned with the future scale of the carrier”.

Some cabin crew were apparently approached in October with proposals involving redundancies or demotions.

Read more: What went wrong for airBaltic? Why the airline filed for Chapter 11 protection Read more: What went wrong for airBaltic? Why the airline filed for Chapter 11 protection

Secondments offered as part of package of efficiencies

Under the proposed arrangement, some pilots have been given the choice of taking up a secondment with Air Niugini.

AirBaltic said the placements were part of a cooperation agreement with Air Niugini and said that participation for its crews would be voluntary. 

The airline did not disclose how many pilots might be involved.

Air Niugini has three Airbus A220-300s in its fleet, leased from Azorra, and an order with Airbus for eight A220-100s. 

The airline was the 25th global operator of the A220, with each wearing a special livery marking the 50th Anniversary of the Independence of Papua New Guinea. 

Fleet reduction accompanies workforce measures

The staffing changes come alongside a substantial reduction in the airline’s planned fleet. 

airBaltic intends to cut its Airbus A220-300 fleet from 54 aircraft to 36 by the end of this year, a reversal of its previous plan to operate 100 aircraft by 2030.

The airline’s financial position has deteriorated following a sharp increase in jet fuel prices after the outbreak of war involving the US, Israel and Iran. 

airBaltic began the year without fuel hedging, which would have helped shield it from the subsequent price rises and which have saved other airlines hundreds of millions in fuel costs.

Majority-owned by the Latvian government, the carrier entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in September. 

airBaltic seeks to minimise redundancies

The airline said discussions with employees remained ongoing and declined to provide figures for the number of staff that might be affected.

A spokesperson said different employee groups had been offered a combination of measures.

“The process is being carried out ​in full compliance with applicable labour laws and regulations, ensuring that all affected employees receive the rights and entitlements provided by law,” a spokesperson was quoted by Reuters as saying.

“Different employee groups have been offered options such ‌as reduced ⁠workloads, alternative roles and transfers between bases, with the aim of minimising the number of redundancies.”

]]> Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian airline to file for bankruptcy: What passengers need to know https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/norse-atlantics-norwegian-airline-to-file-for-bankruptcy/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:04:34 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58224 Norse Atlantic Airways’ Norwegian operating subsidiary is to file for bankruptcy after failing to secure emergency funding, with all flights cancelled and ticket sales halted.

The post Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian airline to file for bankruptcy: What passengers need to know appeared first on AGN.

]]> Norse Atlantic Airways confirmed today (27 November) that its Norwegian operating subsidiary is to file for bankruptcy after attempts to secure enough funding to keep the airline flying failed.

The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has decided to file a bankruptcy petition with Agder District Court in Norway.

The announcement comes just a day after the low-cost long-haul carrier suspended flights while it sought emergency financing.

Norse Atlantic has now cancelled all flights and stopped selling tickets, leaving passengers with existing bookings facing the prospect of having to make alternative travel arrangements.

Norse Atlantic continues efforts to save UK airline

The bankruptcy decision applies to Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating company, rather than the entire airline group.

Its listed parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, and UK operating subsidiary are not included in the announced bankruptcy proceedings.

Chief executive Eivind Roald said work was continuing to find a way for the remaining business to operate.

However, there is currently no confirmed date for flights to resume.

Norse Atlantic fails to secure emergency funding

Norse Atlantic, which began commercial flights in June 2022, had warned on Wednesday that its financial position was critical.

The airline had been in discussions with investors over a potential takeover that would include a financing agreement.

Earlier on Friday, Norse Atlantic revealed it had received lease termination notices covering all 12 of its Boeing 787 Dreamliners. The company disputes the validity of those notices.

What should passengers with Norse Atlantic bookings do?

Passengers with upcoming Norse Atlantic flights should not travel to the airport expecting their flight to operate. Those stranded abroad should look at alternative flights and contact their travel insurer or booking provider.

Whether passengers can recover the cost of their tickets will depend on how they booked, their method of payment and any financial protection in place.

UK passengers who paid by credit card may be protected under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act, while those who paid by debit card may be able to recover their money through chargeback.

Passengers who booked as part of an ATOL-protected package holiday should contact their tour operator.

In the US, the Department of Transportation advises passengers affected by airline bankruptcies to contact their credit card provider or travel insurer if they cannot obtain a refund from the airline.

Passengers should retain booking confirmations, cancellation notices and receipts for replacement flights, accommodation and other expenses in case they need to make a claim.

In a statement to Reuters, the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association said: “This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled.”

]]> Why Thanksgiving Sunday is the busiest day for US airlines and how carriers keep flights moving https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/how-us-airlines-prepare-thanksgiving-sunday-rush/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 13:59:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58147 Thanksgiving Sunday is one of the busiest air travel days in the United States. Here’s how airlines plan aircraft rotations, call in reserve crews and respond when airports have to slow the flow of arrivals.

The post Why Thanksgiving Sunday is the busiest day for US airlines and how carriers keep flights moving appeared first on AGN.

]]> After the US Thanksgiving holiday, many are rushing to get back home, and most fly on Sunday. 

The US Transportation Security Administration expects to screen more than three million people on Sunday, the Thanksgiving holiday’s busiest day at security checkpoints, as Reuters reported. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which counts flights, projected its holiday peak for Tuesday, 24 November, at more than 52,000. 

US carriers are offering an average of 38,000 more seats per day than they did over last year’s Thanksgiving period, according to Airlines for America. Adding a flight means finding room in an aircraft’s rotation. An airline can also put a larger aircraft on a busy route, adding seats without using another take-off or landing slot.

How American Airlines and Southwest prepare for peak Thanksgiving demand

At American, preparations for the Sunday schedule began months ago. At 11 am Central Time on Sunday, November 29 November, American Airlines expects to have 1,130 flights operating at once.

Nearly 500 people will be on duty at its Integrated Operations Centre, where dispatchers, crew schedulers and maintenance teams help keep aircraft moving. American and its regional partners have 7,021 flights planned for Sunday, their biggest operating day since the pandemic.

Southwest’s schedule for Sunday 29 November includes more than 4,600 departures across the network. “The
increase in service on one of the historically busiest travel days of the year gives Customers even
more itinerary options when travelling home from holiday vacations,” the airline stated in its holiday schedule announcement.

How United manages aircraft schedules, spare jets and crew planning

At United’s Denver hub, the work began in August. Jonna McGrath, vice president of the hub, told Denver broadcaster KDVR that the airline started by reviewing its schedule and determining where it would need people and how many.

The carrier expects more than 60,000 customers a day to travel through Denver over the holiday period. It is adding more than 40 round trips the weekend after Thanksgiving and increasing its overnight flying.

An extra round trip means two more departures to staff and another turn at each end. Scheduling teams have to leave time for ground staff to unload bags, clean and service the aircraft and board the next flight. A short turn gives the airline more time to fly the aircraft over the course of the day. It also leaves less room to absorb a delay on the inbound leg.

The more flying an airline schedules for each aircraft, the more departures a single late arrival can affect. At a connecting hub, a late aircraft can also leave passengers and bags racing to make other flights. The overnight schedule matters too. An aircraft may need to finish the day at a particular airport so technicians can work on it before its next departure.

Holding an aircraft in reserve costs flying time but can save a departure if a scheduled jet develops a fault. United’s agreement with regional partner SkyWest requires it to maintain spare regional jets.

The contract also ties overnight maintenance to SkyWest’s existing maintenance locations. A spare still needs to be in reach of the delayed flight, with a qualified crew available to fly it. The SkyWest agreement requires United’s written consent before using a smaller spare.

On a heavily booked flight, the swap could keep the service running while leaving some passengers to be rebooked.

What happens when pilots reach their duty time limits?

A pilot can reach a duty limit while the aircraft is still at the gate. Crew schedulers can call in reserve pilots, provided they are qualified on the aircraft and have enough duty time left for the trip. US rules distinguish between short-call reserve and airport standby. For pilots on airport standby, the time spent waiting already counts towards their flight duty period.

At American’s operations centre, crew schedulers track assignments while dispatchers plan and monitor flights. The duty director brings those teams together on the operations floor. If a delay means an aircraft and its crew will miss their next departure, the airline may be able to swap the aircraft, replace the crew or do both.

Each change also has to work for the flights those people and aircraft were meant to operate later.

At a hub, a late inbound flight can force a decision even when the connecting aircraft and its crew are ready. United showed KDVR how its ConnectionSaver system identifies passengers at risk of missing their onward flight. In the example, travellers arriving from Rapid City were connecting to San Diego.

The system can hold the departure when there is time to do so. A short wait may save those passengers from rebooking, but a longer one can put the outbound aircraft behind schedule.

How airlines respond to FAA ground delays and airport restrictions

Low cloud or strong winds can change which runways an airport can use and how many aircraft it can accept each hour. If demand is expected to exceed that rate for an extended period, the FAA can assign later departure times to inbound flights through a ground delay programme. Holding aircraft at their departure airports reduces the need to queue in the air. A ground stop temporarily prevents affected flights from departing.

The FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Centre coordinates the national response. Airport facilities report how many arrivals and departures they can handle per hour as weather, runway configurations and the mix of aircraft change. FAA procedures also require local traffic managers to review staffing and equipment when planning operations. A Sunday schedule built for clear skies can send more flights to a hub than controllers can accommodate once visibility drops.

A later departure time gives the airline a decision of its own. If the aircraft is still at the gate, it may have to move to free the stand for an arrival. If the delay stretches far enough, the crew scheduler may need to find another pilot or revisit the crew’s next assignment. The same restriction can create a gate problem at one airport and a crew problem at another.

How Delta tests its operational readiness before Thanksgiving.

Even after a restriction lifts, the airline may have aircraft and crews in the wrong cities. Delta described that problem after the nationwide ground stop on 13 November, when departures resumed, but the airline still had to reposition crews and aircraft.

Delta’s winter operations plan starts with what each airport can handle. Before winter, teams at northern hubs and other stations work out how many aircraft they can de-ice per hour under different levels of freezing precipitation, and where on the ramp that work can take place. Delta’s operations centre uses those estimates and its own meteorologists’ forecasts to adjust the schedule when freezing weather is expected.

Delta used another fallback on 22 November, a week before the expected peak. When its automated weight-and-balance system failed, teams calculated the figures manually to get flights moving, the Associated Press reported. A Delta spokesperson said the automated system was fully restored by Monday.

On Thanksgiving Sunday, getting a delayed flight out is only part of the job for airlines. The aircraft and crew also need to be in place for the next one. An aircraft held at the gate may need to move to make room for an arrival. A longer delay may also require another pilot or a change to the crew’s next assignment.

Airlines coordinate these busy periods carefully, but weather can disrupt even the best-made plans. For those flying on Sunday, the best advice is to remember to pack patience.

]]> Portuguese Army receives aviation capability after 74 years with first Black Hawk delivery https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/portuguese-army-receives-first-uh-60l-black-hawk-helicopter/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 13:11:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58184 The Portuguese Army has taken delivery of its first Sikorsky UH-60L Black Hawk at Tancos Military Airfield, ending a 74-year absence of organic crewed aviation and launching a four-aircraft modernisation programme.

The post Portuguese Army receives aviation capability after 74 years with first Black Hawk delivery appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Portuguese Army has received its first Sikorsky UH-60L Black Hawk helicopter, restoring a crewed aviation capability it lost 74 years ago when its aircraft were transferred to the newly established Portuguese Air Force.

The helicopter, the first of a planned fleet of four, was transported from Florida in the United States to Tancos Military Airfield aboard an Embraer KC-390 military transport aircraft operated by the Portuguese Air Force.

The acquisition ends decades of unsuccessful attempts by the Portuguese Army to establish its own helicopter fleet. It will give the service greater control over the movement of troops, battlefield medical evacuation, reconnaissance and logistical support without having to rely entirely on the air force for helicopter operations.

Portugal’s Ministry of National Defence described the arrival as a “historic milestone” in the modernisation of the land forces, strengthening the army’s mobility and operational autonomy.

The helicopter was formally presented at Tancos on 19 November in the presence of Portuguese Defence Minister Nuno Melo and Army Chief of Staff General Eduardo Mendes Ferrao.

The ceremony also marked the unveiling of new ground-based air defence equipment, including the RapidRanger missile system and Ground Master 200 surveillance radar.

Melo described the occasion as “a historic day for the armed forces”, according to Austrian defence publication Militar Aktuell.

A 74-year wait for an army aviation capability

The Portuguese Army has been without its own crewed aircraft since 1952, when the country consolidated its military aviation assets under the newly formed air force.

Efforts to reintroduce aviation within the army began in the 1990s, but successive helicopter procurement programmes fell through.

Portugal cancelled an order for nine EC635 light helicopters in 2002. A separate acquisition of 10 NH90 military transport helicopters, ordered in 2001, also failed to materialise after the government withdrew from the programme in 2012.

The repeated setbacks eventually led to the dissolution of the Army Light Aviation Unit at Tancos in 2015. The unit had never received the helicopters intended for it.

The latest attempt gathered momentum in 2023 when responsibility for the Support, Protection and Evacuation Helicopters programme, known by its Portuguese acronym HAPE, was transferred from the air force to the army under a revision of Portugal’s Military Programming Law.

The NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) took responsibility for the acquisition in 2024.

“Today, we are delivering. We are providing capabilities that have been a long-held aspiration for decades,” Mendes Ferrao said at the unveiling ceremony, as reported by Militar Aktuell.

Former US Army Black Hawks get a new lease of life

Rather than purchasing newly manufactured helicopters, Portugal opted to acquire and modernise former US Army UH-60L airframes.

The aircraft are being refurbished in Florida by the Sahar Group, a US company specialising in the maintenance, modernisation and support of Black Hawk helicopters.

The Portuguese Army announced the contract in July 2026. The agreement includes helicopter refurbishment, the integration of mission-specific equipment, training for pilots and maintenance personnel, and technical support.

The original procurement covers three helicopters with an option for a fourth. However, the army now expects to receive four aircraft by 2028.

The programme represents an investment of approximately €50 million ($55 million), including VAT, infrastructure improvements and personnel training.

According to media reports, the second helicopter is scheduled for delivery in the second quarter of 2027, followed by the third in the corresponding period of 2028.

Digital cockpit and new mission equipment

The UH-60L is an improved version of the original UH-60A Black Hawk, featuring more powerful General Electric T700-GE-701C turboshaft engines and an upgraded transmission.

The twin-engine helicopter can accommodate 11 equipped soldiers in addition to its crew. It has a maximum gross weight of approximately 10,000kg and can carry external loads of up to 4,080kg.

Portugal’s helicopters are undergoing substantial upgrades to their avionics and mission systems.

The original analogue cockpit instruments are being replaced with Moog’s Genesys digital avionics suite and a four-axis autopilot.

The upgraded cockpit incorporates synthetic vision, terrain awareness and warning systems, traffic monitoring and automated hover assistance. These features can reduce pilot workload, particularly during operations in poor visibility or close to the ground.

A Portuguese Army spokesman confirmed that the first helicopter was equipped with two side-mounted machine guns and a forward-looking infrared (FLIR) electro-optical and infrared sensor.

The sensor, housed in a turret beneath the helicopter’s nose, allows crews to observe terrain and objects using thermal imaging as well as conventional imagery.

Black Hawks to support military and civilian operations

The helicopters will be operated by the newly established Helicopter Unit for Support, Protection and Evacuation at Tancos.

Although the primary requirement is to support military operations, Portugal also intends to use the aircraft during natural disasters and other civilian emergencies.

The helicopters will be able to transport emergency response personnel, deliver essential supplies, evacuate casualties and support aerial firefighting.

The equipment being acquired includes rescue hoists, stretchers, external cargo hooks and firefighting buckets with capacities of 2,000 and 2,950 litres.

Wildfire suppression is already among the roles undertaken by the Portuguese Air Force’s Black Hawks, which operate from Ovar.

Currently, the Air Force is equipped with two versions of the helicopter: the UH-60A and the UH-60L.

Building an aviation unit from scratch

Despite the arrival of the first Black Hawk, the Portuguese Army is still some way from establishing a fully operational helicopter unit.

The aircraft has already undertaken test flights, including a demonstration at the unveiling ceremony with Melo and Mendes Ferrao on board. That flight was conducted by a Sahar Group crew.

The first Portuguese Army pilots have undergone training in Spain, while work is continuing at Tancos to modernise hangars, the control tower and other facilities required to support helicopter operations.

Portugal also wants to develop Tancos into a centre for aviation training, maintenance and operational support, working with its air force and allied militaries.

]]> China to showcase upgraded J-20 and Y-20 aircraft at Zhuhai for first time https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/china-j-20a-y-20b-airshow-debut/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:58:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58170 New J-20 fighter and Y-20 transport variants are set to feature for the first time at China's upcoming Airshow China.

The post China to showcase upgraded J-20 and Y-20 aircraft at Zhuhai for first time appeared first on AGN.

]]> Newer variants of China’s J-20 stealth fighter and Y-20 military transport aircraft are set to appear at next month’s Airshow China for the first time. Earlier variants have previously appeared at other events in China.

Airshow China is officially known as the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province.

China’s improved J-20A stealth fighter to appear at airshow

China’s state-run English news outlet, Global Times, reported that a Chengdu J-20A ‘Mighty Dragon’ 5th-generation fighter jet will make its first flight performance at December’s Airshow China.

Global Times writes, “The J-20A’s appearance will mark its first flight demonstration at Airshow China, offering visitors a closer look at an upgraded version of China’s fifth-generation stealth fighter.”

The J-20A variant was previously publicly unveiled at a military parade in Beijing in September 2025. While that was its first official appearance, the J-20A had been spotted since December 2022.

The Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping claimed to the Global Times that the J-20A is a major upgrade over the original J-20 variant.

It comes with improvements to its avionics, flight-control, and fire-control systems intended to strengthen its situational awareness and overall combat capabilities. It is powered by domestic Chinese WS-15 engines in place of earlier Chinese WS-10 and the very early Russian engines.

First appearance of China’s Y-20B airlifter at Airshow China

The stealth fighter is to be joined by a Xi’an Y-20B ‘Chubby Girl’ strategic airlifter that will be placed on static display for the first time. The variant is an upgraded version of China’s domestically developed large military transport aircraft.

The Y-20 family of airlifters is commonly compared with the Boeing C-17 Globemaster III, although there are notable differences.

Its cargo hold will also be open to visitors, allowing them to see its cargo hold. Song says the airlifter helps to highlight China’s growing confidence in developing and manufacturing strategic airlifters.

Song said the Y-20B’s most significant upgrade is replacing the older Y-20A’s Russian-made D-30KP-2 turbofan engines with China’s domestic WS-20 high-bypass-ratio turbofan engines.

The airlifter is to be joined by its YY-20A aerial refueling variant. It is able to carry China’s heaviest Type 99A or Type 99B main battle tanks.

China’s J-20 enters its next phase with air superiority and MUM-T upgrades China’s J-20 enters its next phase with air superiority and MUM-T upgrades

Other aircraft taking part in Airshow China

Overall, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force is set to showcase more than 60 pieces of equipment, covering 33 types of equipment between 7 and 13 December. Some will be static displays, while others will be conducting flight demonstrations.

The J-20 will be joined by China’s second stealth fighter, the Shenyang J-35A, which was first unveiled at an airshow in China in November 2024.

Another fighter set to make an appearance is the Shenyang J-16 ‘Hidden Dragon.’ The J-16 is a Chinese-designed and built land-based fighter jet derived from the Su-30MKK.

Other notable static-display items include the H-6K bomber, the J-20C fighter, and the WZ-10 UAV. Not all of the aircraft have been confirmed yet.

Besides aircraft, the PLAAF will display a new-generation early-warning radar system and other unspecified equipment. 

Flight demonstrations at Airshow China will see performances by China’s Bayi aerobatic team alongside Russia’s Russian Knights and the UAE Air Force’s Al Fursan aerobatic team.

]]> Norse Atlantic faces loss of entire 787 fleet as lessors issue termination notices https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/norse-atlantic-latest-787-fleet-lessors-termination-notices/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:03:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58179 Norse has said it is contesting "the validity of the termination notices”.

The post Norse Atlantic faces loss of entire 787 fleet as lessors issue termination notices appeared first on AGN.

]]> The future for Norse Atlantic looked even more grim on Friday after the struggling carrier’s aircraft lessors issued lease termination notices for all 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet.

In a statement, the Norway based low-cost long-haul carrier confirmed it had received “notices from its aircraft lessors for the termination of lease agreements for all 12 aircraft in the Norse fleet.”

Norse said it was contesting “the validity of the termination notices”.

Norse suspends all flights after warning of ‘critical’ financial state

On Thursday, the airline suspended all flights and warned it would file for bankruptcy if it could not find a short-term solution to its financing woes.

Two of its 787s were seen parked up in a remote area of London Gatwick airport, which was the carrier’s largest operating base. FlightRadar24 reported that two Norse 787s (G-CKOF and G-CKWD) had flight plans filed for the aircraft long-term storage airport of Teruel, Spain, in the coming hours.

A day earlier, the carrier issued a warning that its financial situation was “critical”.

Read more: What could happen to Norse Atlantic’s Boeing 787 Dreamliners? Read more: What could happen to Norse Atlantic’s Boeing 787 Dreamliners?

In its latest update on Friday, Norse stated again that the company was continuing to speak with potential creditors to secure short-term financing. 

But it also added: “There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found. Further information will be provided as and when appropriate.”

Loss of low-cost long-haul from UK airports

Norse Atlantic’s flight suspension affects seven routes, including five linking the airline with Thailand. 

The carrier had been due to further expand its network next month, with new Manchester-Bangkok and London Gatwick-Phuket routes scheduled to begin in December.

In a statement, Norse apologised to customers affected by the cancellations but did not clarify how refunds or alternative travel would be handled. 

Just a year ago, Norse was boasting of load factors of 99% and “significant passenger growth”.

However the reality of operating in a high-fuel-cost environment and with many parts of the world off-limits or with restricted over-flight rights has taken its toll.

Pakistan International Airlines replaces Norse wet-leased aircraft with its own fleet

The suspension also disrupted Pakistan International Airlines’ (PIA) UK operations, which had been supplemented by two Boeing 787-9s supplied by Norse Atlantic under a wet-lease arrangement agreed in October.

Under the deal, Norse was responsible for providing the aircraft and their crews, as well as maintenance and insurance. The first Dreamliner was delivered to Islamabad on 1 November.

Read more: What went wrong for Norse Atlantic? How the dream unravelled Read more: What went wrong for Norse Atlantic? How the dream unravelled

PIA said passengers at London Heathrow and Manchester were already preparing to board when it received the news that Norse was suspending all flights.

The resulting cancellations affected PK786, the Heathrow-Islamabad service, and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore.

PIA said it would remove the leased aircraft from its UK operation and operate the full schedule using its own Boeing 777s.

]]> US Navy doubles test fleet of next-generation ‘doomsday planes’ with $1.13bn contract https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/us-navy-e130j-test-fleet-expansion/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 11:37:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58118 The US Navy has formally exercised its option to double its next-gen TACAMO test fleet to six as it plans to increase the operational fleet to 25 from the 16 in service today.

The post US Navy doubles test fleet of next-generation ‘doomsday planes’ with $1.13bn contract appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Pentagon has awarded Northrop Grumman a $1.1 billion contract to double its ‘doomsday’ E-130J fleet.

This comes after Pentagon reports revealed that the US Navy may double its planned acquisition of E-130J Phoenix II aircraft for its Take Charge And Move Out (TACAMO).

US Navy doubles E-130J test fleet

The United States Department of War has awarded Northrop Grumman a “$1,130,397,498 cost-plus-incentive-fee modification” to the existing E-130J delivery contract.

The extra funding exercises options for another three E-130J test articles and initial spares in support of engineering and manufacturing development. This doubles the future E-130J fleet from the three previously contracted to six now.

.@LockheedMartin will deliver high-fidelity training devices and services for the E-130J Phoenix II, leveraging its proven C-130J expertise. They join the @northropgrumman industry team supporting the @USNavy Take Charge and Move Out (TACAMO) mission. Click for more:

— Lockheed Martin News (@LMNews) April 29, 2026

The contract states, “The E-130J program will integrate specialized, secure communications systems into government-furnished C-130J-30 aircraft to recapitalize the Navy’s Take Charge and Move Out strategic communications mission. “

The programme expects to complete the work by January 2030 and is based on the stretched Lockheed Martin C-130J-30 Super Hercules turboprop.

Role of E-130Js and the need to replace ageing E-6B Mercury fleet

The existing E-6B Mercury and incoming E-130J Phoenix II TACAMO fleets can be understood as serving a sort of communication relay function.

TACAMO provides aerial command and control support for nuclear ballistic missile submarines. They have the ability to transmit orders to launch nuclear strikes while they are submerged.

Due to their role in launching nuclear strikes, they are one of the aircraft types commonly dubbed ‘doomsday planes.’

Similar to the KC-135 Stratotanker and the E-3 Sentry radar plane, the Boeing E-6 Mercury is based on the old Boeing 707 lineage, specifically the Boeing 707-300.

Military aircraft are often based on already old commercial aircraft; e.g., the future E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center (SAOC) will be based on the Boeing 747-8.

The final Boeing 707 commercial passenger flight in the US took place in 1983, while the first E-6 Mercury was delivered to the Navy in 1989. So while these aircraft are not as old as their commercial US-based counterparts, they are still around 37 years old and increasingly difficult to maintain.

The Boeing 707-based TACAMO aircraft replaced an older generation of legacy C-130-based aircraft.

US upgrades E-6B Mercury TACAMO nuclear aircraft despite looming replacement US upgrades E-6B Mercury TACAMO nuclear aircraft despite looming replacement

US Navy planning to double its E-130J programme

In August, it was reported that the US Navy plans to double the number of aircraft to perform the TACAMO mission. A released Pentagon report suggested it was intending to acquire 31 E-130J Phoenix II aircraft to replace its 16 ageing E-6B Mercury aircraft.

But while the E-130 is to take over the core TACAMO role, it is not planned to inherit all of the E-6’s roles, including the Looking Glass / ABNCP / airborne launch-control roles for land-based ICBMs and bombers.

Those roles are expected to be handled by other US Air Force programmes such as the SAOC or a Looking Glass-Next programme. The decision is deliberate to make the C-130J-based design practical by reducing the retired mission systems, size, and complexity.

The decision to increase the fleet from 16 to 25 (plus six test articles) is primarily for greater resilience, dispersal, and operational margin on a more austere-capable platform.

The Navy took delivery of its first C-130J-30 airframe destined to become an E-130J Phoenix in October 2026. The aircraft will now be modified with its new systems. The exact planned entry into operational service for the E-130J remains classified.

]]> Leonardo rolls out first M-346 for Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/leonardo-m-346-frecce-tricolori/ Fri, 27 Nov 2026 10:15:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58126 Leonardo has rolled out the first of 15 custom M-346 PAN jets for Italy’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team, initiating flight tests ahead of 2027–2028 deliveries to replace the legacy MB-339 fleet.

The post Leonardo rolls out first M-346 for Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team appeared first on AGN.

]]> Leonardo has rolled out the first of 15 specially configured M-346 aircraft for the Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team, marking the beginning of flight testing ahead of deliveries between 2027 and 2028.

The twin-engine aircraft will replace the Aermacchi MB-339 PAN, which has carried the Italian national aerobatic team through more than four decades of displays at home and abroad.

Announcing the milestone on 26 November, Leonardo said the programme was progressing on schedule, with pilot and technician training underway alongside the development of a new aerobatic display routine tailored to the capabilities of the M-346.

Designated M-346 PAN by the Italian Air Force, the aircraft will be manufactured at Leonardo’s production facility in Venegono Superiore, in the northern Italian province of Varese.

The programme also includes technical and logistical support, flight simulators, maintenance training systems and infrastructure upgrades at Rivolto Air Base in Udine, home to the Italian Air Force’s 313th Aerobatic Training Squadron.

“This programme represents a major success for Leonardo and for Italy,” said Lorenzo Mariani, chief executive and general manager of Leonardo.

“Our close collaboration with the Italian Air Force and the Italian Ministry of Defence has enabled us to achieve this important milestone, laying the foundations for further achievements.”

Frecce Tricolori prepares to bid farewell to the MB-339

The selection of the M-346 as the future aircraft of the Frecce Tricolori was unveiled on 12 September 2024 at Istrana Air Base near Treviso, during a ceremony marking the team’s return from its North American tour.

The transition represents a significant technological leap for the Italian aerobatic team, which will move from a single-engine jet trainer of an earlier generation to a twin-engine aircraft equipped with digital avionics and electronic flight controls.

The M-346 also offers different performance and manoeuvrability characteristics, giving the team scope to develop new formations and aerobatic sequences.

“It is a truly moving experience to see this remarkable achievement of Italian technology take to the skies,” said Lieutenant General Antonio Conserva, Chief of Staff of the Italian Air Force.

“The transition from the illustrious MB-339 to the M-346 marks another step forward, embracing the challenges of the future while remaining true to the values that have always defined the Frecce Tricolori,” he said.

The new aircraft features a livery styled by Italian design house Pininfarina. The design combines a predominantly dark blue finish with sweeping green, white and red stripes representing the Italian flag.

“The Italian flag that we will continue to fly in skies around the world symbolises our national unity, the professionalism of the men and women of the Italian Air Force and the wider defence community, as well as our country’s ingenuity, creativity, and technological and industrial excellence,”Lt. Gen. Conserva added.

How the M-346 has been adapted for aerobatic displays

Although the M-346 PAN retains the avionics, digital flight controls and performance characteristics of the advanced jet trainer, Leonardo has introduced several modifications specifically for the aerobatic team.

These include a smoke generation system, which will allow the Frecce Tricolori to continue painting the skies with its distinctive green, white and red smoke trails.

The aircraft also incorporates video streaming equipment, modifications to the cockpit and flight control systems, and auxiliary fuel tanks to support flights between display venues.

An onboard access ladder will allow pilots to enter and leave the cockpit without relying on external boarding equipment, a useful addition when operating from different airfields during international tours.

One of the most significant differences between the M-346 and its predecessor is its quadruple-redundant fly-by-wire flight control system.

Instead of relying on conventional mechanical connections between the cockpit controls and the aircraft’s control surfaces, the system uses electronic signals and flight control computers to interpret the pilot’s commands.

Multiple independent channels provide redundancy in the event of a system failure.

The introduction of the aircraft will require the team’s pilots to familiarise themselves with its handling characteristics before developing and rehearsing a new display programme.

From advanced fighter training to formation aerobatics

The M-346 was developed to prepare military pilots for the transition to modern frontline fighter aircraft.

The twin-seat jet combines a digital cockpit with a high degree of manoeuvrability, allowing trainee pilots to experience many of the flight characteristics and cockpit demands associated with contemporary combat aircraft.

Much of the M-346’s appeal as a military trainer lies in its ability to combine actual flying with computer-generated combat scenarios.

Its Embedded Tactical Training System (ETTS) allows pilots to train against simulated threats and practise tactical missions without requiring additional aircraft to represent adversaries.

The aircraft forms the backbone of the International Flight Training School (IFTS) at Decimomannu in Sardinia, established through a partnership between Leonardo and the Italian Air Force.

The school combines airborne instruction with ground-based flight simulators, mission planning systems and computer-generated scenarios.

Known as Live, Virtual and Constructive (LVC) training, the technology allows pilots flying actual aircraft to participate in exercises alongside pilots operating ground-based simulators and entirely computer-generated forces.

While the requirements of an aerobatic team differ considerably from those of a fighter training school, the Frecce Tricolori will benefit from the aircraft’s established training and simulation infrastructure.

Leonardo also sees the selection of the M-346 by the Italian aerobatic team as an opportunity to broaden the aircraft’s international market beyond advanced military training and light combat operations.

“The M-346 is now well positioned to pursue major new commercial and industrial cooperation opportunities worldwide, both as a trainer and multirole aircraft and as a platform for aerobatic teams,” said Stefano Bortoli, managing director of Leonardo’s Aircraft Division.

A new aircraft carrying an Italian tradition

The Frecce Tricolori’s international appearances have long provided a showcase for Italian aircraft manufacturing as well as the flying skills of the country’s military pilots.

Mariani acknowledged the contribution of the workforce involved in developing the team’s new aircraft.

“Behind every aircraft are designers, engineers, technicians, skilled workers and entire industrial supply chains,” he said. “Behind it are investments in research and development, expertise and a culture of industrial excellence and dedication that is passed down through generations and continually renewed.”

Conserva also highlighted the relationship between the Italian Air Force and the country’s aerospace industry.

“Behind every new chapter in the history of the Frecce Tricolori lies an extraordinary wealth of expertise, passion and professionalism shared by Italian Air Force personnel and the skilled workforce of our national industry,” he said. “This heritage is built on education, training and the ability to work together as a team.”

Although production and deliveries are scheduled between 2027 and 2028, Leonardo has not specified when the Frecce Tricolori will perform its first full public display with the M-346 or when the last MB-339 PAN will be retired.

 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;

.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;

.sie-hdr__logo-img {

 display: block;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;

 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}
 .lh-hero .lh-title{margin:0 0 12px}
 .lh-hero .lh-subtitle{margin:0;max-width:52ch}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{position:relative;z-index:1;margin:clamp(14px,1.8vw,22px) 0 0;gap:10px 24px}
 /* The bar itself carries the emphasis: taller, larger type, and a navy
 action instead of the yellow one — yellow reads promotional, and on warm
 paper it was the loudest thing in the hero. Scoped to .lh-herosearch so
 the same widget elsewhere keeps the brand button. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-bar{min-height:64px;padding:4px 6px 4px 14px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-input{font-size:17px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn{background:#12233D;border-color:#12233D;color:#fff;font-weight:600}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn:hover{background:#1E3354;border-color:#1E3354}
 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}
 /* The flow view (AI matching on) groups results into one .sie-flow__branch
 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.
 The first keeps padding-left:0 so its numeral lines up with the margin
 the hero headline uses. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-num{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(27px,2.9vw,40px);font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;line-height:1.05;color:#12233D;background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}
 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}
 @media(max-width:700px){
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr))}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:nth-child(2){border-right:0}
 }
 /* Monogram instead of a repeated building glyph. Hairline tile, serif
 letters — it reads as a placeholder somebody chose, not as missing data. */
 .lh-uni-logo-placeholder{display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;background:#F4F2ED;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:5px;color:#8A8578}
 .lh-uni-monogram{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:22px;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:1px;color:#12233D}
 /* ── For institutions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
 The one full navy band on the page. It is dark on purpose: it marks a
 change of audience, so a student scrolling past knows at a glance that
 this part is not addressed to them. */
 .lh-inst{background:#12233D;color:#fff}
 .lh-inst-wrap *,.lh-inst-wrap *::before,.lh-inst-wrap *::after{box-sizing:border-box}
 .lh-inst-inner{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:clamp(48px,6vw,88px) clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.35fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:clamp(28px,4vw,64px);align-items:start}
 .lh-inst-badge{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-h{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(26px,3.1vw,40px);line-height:1.16;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;color:#fff;max-width:20ch}
 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}
 .lh-inst-actions{margin:0;display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px}
 .lh-inst-btn{display:inline-block;text-decoration:none;background:#fff;color:#12233D;font-size:15.5px;font-weight:600;padding:14px 26px;border:1px solid #fff;border-radius:4px;min-height:44px}
 .lh-inst-btn:hover{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#44597A;font-weight:500}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost:hover{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-terms{margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none}
 .lh-inst-terms li{border-top:1px solid #28405F;padding:20px 0}
 .lh-inst-terms li:first-child{border-top:0;padding-top:0}
 .lh-inst-k{margin:0 0 6px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:19px;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-v{margin:0;font-size:15px;line-height:1.6;color:#C6D2E0}
 @media(max-width:860px){
 .lh-inst-inner{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 }
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-heroalt{flex-direction:row;flex-wrap:wrap}
 .lh-heroalt-card{flex:1 1 220px}
 .lh-hero-scrim{background:linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(250,248,244,.97) 0%,rgba(250,248,244,.93) 62%,rgba(250,248,244,.72) 100%)}
 }
 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
 /* The accent word: italic navy reads editorial; bright orange read promo. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-gradient-text{color:#12233D;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D;font-style:italic;font-weight:600}
 /* One label above the headline is enough. The H1 eyebrow ("STUDY IN
 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}
 /* Phones: the hero had no side gutter, so the eyebrow sat flush against
 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text,.lh-hero .lh-subtitle{text-align:left}
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 }
 /* ── Section headers: same voice as the institutions band ─────────────
 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-header h2{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px) !important;letter-spacing:-.4px;line-height:1.15;color:#12233D !important}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-how{background:#FAF8F4}
 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 /* How it works: the three steps were top-aligned, so the middle card
 (longer text) hung lower than its neighbours. Stretch evens them. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-steps{align-items:stretch}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step{background:#fff;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-num{background:#12233D;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-weight:500}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-icon{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D;border-radius:6px}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-arrow{color:#B7B1A5}
 /* Cards: tighter corners and hairlines everywhere. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card{border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px;border-color:#E4E0D8;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it
 the loudest part of the page. Same content, one navy, warm neutrals.
 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__source-pill{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;box-shadow:none !important;border-radius:4px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch{--branch-color:#12233D !important;--branch-bg:#F4F2ED !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-accent{display:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-icon{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card{background:#FAF8F4;border:1px solid #EDEAE3;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card:hover{border-color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel
 (blue / yellow / blue) via !important rules at .lh-uni-card:nth-child()
 specificity, so this needs one more class to win. Plain paper, so the
 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue
 at 15% so the copy on top keeps full contrast. The right edge fades out

 hairline seams between neighbouring countries; opacity sits on the <svg> itself so overlapping strokes cannot add up into darker lines. */

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {

 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {

 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {

 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {

 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;

 }

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

</ul>

At Omegga, we develop spectral intelligence: we combine AI and spectroscopy to make the invisible visible. Today, our technology is the world's earliest commercially available in-ovo sex determination and is already running in live production. As a B2B company, we work directly with hatcheries, and our focus is on scaling performance, robustness, and deployment across an international customer base. Beyond this first application, our platform enables non-invasive material analysis across biological and industrial environments, from agriculture to food production and beyond.

About us

Workerbase builds the operating system for the shopfloor: software that guides and coordinates the work of people in factories. Manufacturing and logistics companies use it to digitalize their processes in production, maintenance and quality. Our customers include international groups from automotive, steel and the supplier industry. We run the platform as a managed service on our own container infrastructure and support customers who host it themselves. We are ISO 27001 certified and hold a TISAX label.

Your role

You join a small platform team and share responsibility with our Senior DevOps Engineer for running, securing and developing our infrastructure. You are not the "security person on the sidelines". You run the platform and build security straight into pipelines, clusters and processes.

What you'll do

  • Operations: You run and develop our production container orchestration clusters: provisioning, upgrades, scaling, cost.

  • Deployments: You manage customer instances the GitOps way: declarative, versioned and reproducible. That covers rollouts, version management and migrations, in our clusters and in customers' on-prem environments.

  • Infrastructure as code: You develop our infrastructure as code, so every change is reviewed, versioned and repeatable.

  • Security: You build security into the platform, pipelines and processes, from vulnerability management to the secure configuration of clusters and workloads.

  • CI/CD: You develop our build and delivery pipelines, including automated quality and security checks.

  • Observability and on-call: You look after monitoring and alerting, take part in the on-call rotation, handle incidents and write post-mortems.

  • Backup and disaster recovery: You make sure data from our databases and object storage is backed up and can actually be restored when it matters.

  • Compliance: You provide the technical input for ISO 27001 and other security requirements from our customers.

  • Collaboration: You advise the development teams on architecture, security, containerization and deployments, and give technical support to customers who host the platform themselves.

What you bring

  • Several years of experience running container orchestration platforms in production, not just deploying to them

  • Confident with GitOps, declarative deployments and infrastructure as code

  • A practical understanding of security: container hardening, access control, network segmentation, secrets management, vulnerability management, least privilege

  • Experience building and maintaining CI/CD pipelines

About Us

Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies is a joint venture between two industry leaders with a clear vision for automotive’s next chapter. From operating systems to zonal controllers to cloud and connectivity solutions, we’re addressing the challenges of electric vehicles through technology that will set the standards for software-defined vehicles around the world.

The road to the future is uncharted. By combining our expertise across connectivity, AI, security and more, we’ll map a new way forward. Working together, we’ll create a future that’s more connected, more intelligent, more sustainable for everyone.

Role Summary

The Berlin team is looking for a Staff Software Engineer - Infotainment, to provide hands-on technical leadership for complex embedded software and hardware/software integration work. You will help shape architectures that connect vehicle hardware, embedded operating systems, platform services, communication paths, and user-facing behavior into reliable products.

This is a broad technical role for an engineer who can move comfortably between system-level design and implementation. You will work across current and next-generation vehicle platforms, helping teams take ideas from early architecture through development, integration, validation, and production readiness. You’ll be working in a high-performing forward-deployed team working closely with key OEM stakeholders. Examples include physical input, HMI systems and bespoke in-vehicle touchpoints.

This role is based in our Berlin office and requires a minimum of three days per week onsite.

  • Architect, design, develop, and maintain embedded software across hardware interfaces, operating-system services, middleware, communication paths, and applications, using C/C++ and contributing to Rust adoption where it improves safety, reliability, maintainability, or service boundaries.

  • Lead technical design discussions and translate ambiguous requirements into clear interfaces, ownership boundaries, acceptance criteria, dependencies, delivery plans, reusable abstractions, and configuration contracts that scale across vehicle platforms, products, and variants.

  • Evaluate and optimize constrained systems for CPU, memory, storage, power, latency, startup, concurrency, and fault handling while ensuring predictable behavior, reliability, and maintainability.

    At Heim, we are reinventing how healthcare is delivered.

    We believe that healthcare is best delivered in the home of patients, and that we are at the cusp of a systemic shift away from hospital based care.     The Opportunity

    As our Head of Revenue & Commercial Operations, you will build the commercial operating engine that enables ANYbotics to scale.

    Working directly with our CRO and closely with Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Finance and Operations, you will create the processes, insights and operating rhythms that help us make better commercial decisions and execute consistently across regions.

You will have the opportunity to shape that model rather than inherit a finished function, establishing strong foundations and building the Revenue & Commercial Operations capability around you over time.

    This is not a pure strategy role. We are looking for someone who enjoys identifying what needs to improve, designing a practical solution and then getting close enough to the detail to make it happen.


    The Market & Our Technology

    ANYbotics transforms industrial environments in the energy, process, and utility sectors by introducing robotics to applications previously beyond reach. Our mobile robot, ANYmal, uses legs for extreme mobility in complex environments, camera- and LIDAR-based sensing for full autonomy, and AI for high-quality inspection results.

    Our customers are some of the world’s largest asset operators and industrial companies. Their buying journeys are complex, often involving technical validation, business-value assessment, deployment planning and multiple stakeholders before expanding from an initial installation to larger fleets across sites and regions.

    That creates a particularly interesting commercial operations challenge. Scaling ANYbotics requires connecting the traditional disciplines of Revenue Operations with the operational realities of selling, deploying and supporting a physical technology platform.


    About Us

    ANYbotics is a leading robotics company developing autonomous mobile robots for industrial inspection. Our technology enables customers to automate routine inspection work in environments that are complex, hazardous or difficult for people to access.

    Headquartered in Zurich and with a growing international presence, we bring together more than 200 people from across the world spanning robotics, software, hardware, product, operations and commercial functions.

    We are scaling quickly as industrial customers move from initial deployments towards broader adoption of autonomous inspection across their operations.


    Your Contributions

  • Build a trusted commercial forecast: Own and continuously improve sales and revenue forecasting, pipeline governance and visibility of risk, giving Sales leadership, Finance and the executive team a reliable view of performance.

  • Create a scalable commercial operating model: Define and improve sales stages, opportunity standards, customer engagement processes and CRM discipline so teams operate consistently across regions.
